say.straight: In most clubs you play from a usb in the cdjs. rekordbox's export mode is where you prepare it.
say.eli5: In clubs, djs bring their music on a little usb stick. A program gets the stick ready.

say.mentor:
First import your tracks, and the software analyses each one. Then check the beat grids against the waveforms and fix any that are off. Then set your cue points at the moments you'll want, like the intro, the drop, the breakdown and the outro. Then organise your playlists. Then export to the usb.
Last, check it. Plug it into a cdj and make sure the tracks and playlists are there.
say.straight: Import and analyse. Check grids. Set cue points. Organise playlists. Export to usb. Then check it on a cdj.
say.eli5: Add your songs, check their beat marks, mark the good bits, put them in lists, copy them to the stick, then test the stick.

deeper.title: why grids come first
deeper.say: Sync locks to the beat grid, and cue points placed on the beat depend on it too. A wrong grid makes both wrong, so fix grids before anything else.

deeper.title: two usb drives
deeper.say: Always bring two, with the same music on each. Usb drives fail at the worst moments. If one does, you plug in the other and the night carries on.

say.mentor:
Before you export a set, play through the handover you're planning one last time. Your song on deck a, your next track on deck b: pick it from the bank.
Check they sit together at your tempo, check the keys don't clash, run the blend with the faders and the low knobs. If anything sounds off, this is where you fix it, not in the booth.
say.straight: Run your planned handover once before exporting. Pick deck b, check tempo and key, run the blend. Fix problems now, not at the gig.
say.eli5: Before you copy your songs to the stick, try mixing your song into the next one. If something sounds wrong, fix it now.

steps.q: Which order is right?
options: import, check grids, set cues, organise, export
steps.why: Each step leans on the one before it.

whyWrong.1: There's nothing to export yet.
whyWrong.2: You can't set cues on a track you haven't imported.
whyWrong.3: Analysis has to come first.

steps.q: Why check grids before you export?
options: sync and on-beat cues depend on the grid
steps.why: A wrong grid puts sync and your cues in the wrong place.

whyWrong.1: File size isn't affected.
whyWrong.2: Grids are about beats, not key.
whyWrong.3: A bad grid follows you to the club.

steps.q: Why bring two usb drives?
options: one can fail, and the other is your backup
one is for the other dj
steps.why: Hardware fails at the worst moments.

whyWrong.1: One usb works across the players.
whyWrong.3: It's your own insurance.

steps.next: Back to the song path: key and harmonic mixing.

lessons.title: harmonic mixing in practice

song.why: a key that fits lets your song sing into the next track, and one that fights turns the blend sour

lessons.learn: Using the Camelot wheel on real choices: two keys that fit your song, one that clashes, and when a clash is the point.
youCan: find keys that fit your song
hear a key clash
say what one step clockwise does

say.mentor: Two tracks in keys that fit. Their notes sit together, so the blend sounds like one piece of music. Pick a key that fights and the same blend turns sour, even with perfect beats. Harmonic mixing is choosing the next track so that doesn't happen.
say.straight: Fitting keys blend into one sound. Clashing keys sound sour, even with matched beats.
say.eli5: Some songs sound nice together and some sound yucky together, even when the beats match.

say.mentor:
On the Camelot wheel, the same number with the other letter is the relative major or minor: the same notes, a different mood. One step round with the same letter is a fifth away, a smooth move. One step clockwise, up a number, gives a small lift in energy that the crowd feels without knowing why.
It's a tool, not a law. Sometimes a clash at the right moment is exactly the jolt a set needs.
say.straight: Same number, other letter: same notes, different mood. One step with the same letter: smooth. One step clockwise: a small lift. Break the rules when the moment wants it.
say.eli5: Same number: very friendly. Next number: friendly too, and going up feels a bit more exciting.

deeper.title: key shift on the deck
deeper.say: Cdjs can also move a track's key in small steps without changing its tempo, using master tempo and a semitone shift. That's the next lesson.

say.mentor:
Your song's key code is on deck a. Tap through the bank and find two tracks that fit: the screen says fits.
Then find one that clashes and listen to it against your song. Hear the sourness? End on one that fits.
say.straight: Find two bank tracks that fit your song's key and one that clashes. Listen to each. Finish on one that fits.
say.eli5: Find two songs the screen says fit, and one it says clash. Listen. Then pick one that fits.

steps.q: Your song is 8A. Which key gives a small lift?
steps.why: One step clockwise with the same letter.

whyWrong.1: That fits, but it's a step the other way.
whyWrong.2: That's the same key, no lift.
whyWrong.3: That's too far round the wheel.

steps.q: What do 8A and 8B have in common?
options: the same notes, one minor and one major
steps.why: Relative minor and major share their notes.

whyWrong.1: Codes are about key, not tempo.
whyWrong.2: They're as close as keys get.
whyWrong.3: The code says nothing about who made it.

steps.q: Should you always follow the wheel?
options: no, sometimes a clash is the moment
only at the start of a set
steps.why: It's a tool. A deliberate clash can be the jolt a set needs.

whyWrong.1: Rules are there to understand, then sometimes break.
whyWrong.2: It's about all the notes, not just vocals.
whyWrong.3: It applies all night.

steps.next: Back to the song path: cue points and loops.

lessons.title: key shift and master tempo

song.why: when the perfect next track is one step from your song's key, a small shift makes it fit

lessons.learn: Master tempo, which keeps a track's key steady when you change its speed, and key shift, which moves the key without touching the speed.
youCan: say what master tempo does
say how far you can shift a key before it sounds wrong
match a track's tempo without changing its key

say.mentor:
Low, then high. The same note, shifted. On an old turntable, speeding a record up also raised its pitch, so matching tempos bent the key.
Modern decks have master tempo, also called key lock. Change the speed and the key stays where it is.
say.straight: Speeding a record up used to raise its pitch. Master tempo (key lock) keeps the key steady while the tempo changes.
say.eli5: Speeding up an old record made it sound higher. New dj players have a button that keeps the notes the same when you change the speed.

say.mentor:
Key shift does the opposite. It moves the key up or down in semitones, the smallest step between two notes, and leaves the tempo alone. If the track you want is one step from fitting your song, shift it.
Keep it small. One or two semitones usually sounds natural. Go further and you hear it, especially on vocals: chipmunk going up, sluggish going down.
say.straight: Key shift moves the key in semitones without changing tempo. One or two is fine. More and you hear it, especially on vocals.
say.eli5: You can also make a song a little higher or lower without changing its speed. Just a little, or it sounds funny.

deeper.title: with master tempo off
deeper.say: With master tempo off, the pitch fader changes speed and key together. Slow a track down to match and it goes flatter. Speed it up and it goes sharper. That's why djs usually leave master tempo on while beatmatching.

say.mentor:
Deck b's key clashes with your song. Instead of choosing another track, shift deck b's key. Each press of key b moves it a semitone, and the badge shows its new Camelot code.
Find a shift where it fits, then match the tempo. Small shifts, one or two semitones, keep the track sounding natural; big ones start to sound odd. That's key shift.
say.straight: Shift deck b's key a semitone at a time until it fits your song, then match the tempo. Small shifts sound most natural.
say.eli5: Make deck b's song a little higher or lower until it fits yours.

steps.q: What does master tempo do?
options: keeps the key steady while the tempo changes
locks the tempo so it can't change
steps.why: Speed and key come apart, so beatmatching doesn't bend the key.

whyWrong.1: The tempo still moves.
whyWrong.3: That's sync.

steps.q: How far can you usually shift a key before it sounds wrong?
steps.why: Small shifts sound natural. Bigger ones are audible, especially on vocals.

whyWrong.1: You can go further than that.
whyWrong.2: That's far enough to hear clearly.
whyWrong.3: Big shifts sound processed.

steps.q: Master tempo is off and you slow a track down. What happens to its key?
options: it jumps to the relative minor
steps.why: Without key lock, slower also means lower.

whyWrong.1: That's only with master tempo on.
whyWrong.2: Sharper is what happens when you speed it up.
whyWrong.3: It slides down, it doesn't jump.

steps.next: Back to the song path: cue points and loops.

lessons.title: performance looping and hot cues

song.why: a hot cue lets you jump straight to your song's best moment, landing on the one

lessons.learn: Hot cues as performance buttons, loop halving to build tension, and landing a jump right on the one.
youCan: say what a hot cue does
say how halving a loop builds tension
bring a part in on bar one of a phrase

say.mentor: A phrase going round. Now picture a button that jumps the track straight to its drop, mid song, on the beat. That's a hot cue: a saved spot in a track that playback jumps to the instant you press it. Djs use them to rearrange tracks live, while the crowd dances.
say.straight: A hot cue is a saved spot in a track you can jump to instantly. Djs use them to rearrange tracks live.
say.eli5: A hot cue is a button that jumps the song straight to a part you saved, like the best bit.

say.mentor:
Hot cue jumping: hop between sections to build a new arrangement on the fly. Loop halving: loop four bars, then two, then one, then a single beat. Each halving repeats faster, the tension climbs, then you let go into the drop. Cue juggling: flick between two cues quickly for a rhythmic stutter.
All of it feels easy on its own and hard under pressure. Practise until your hands do it without you.
say.straight: Jump between hot cues to rearrange a track. Halve a loop again and again to build tension. Flick between two cues for a stutter. Practise before you try it live.
say.eli5: Jump around a song with the cue buttons. Make a loop shorter and shorter to make it exciting, then let go.

deeper.title: the slicer
deeper.say: Some decks have a slicer, which cuts a loop into segments and plays them back in sequence, ready for you to rearrange.

say.mentor:
Hot cues are bookmarks in a track. Deck b has four: the intro, where the hats come in, the break and the drop. Tap one and deck b jumps there instantly, in time.
Play with them: jump to the break, then to the drop right on the one. That's how djs remix live, jumping between parts of a track. Tap at least two.
say.straight: Four hot cues on deck b: intro, hats in, break, drop. Tap them to jump, in time. Try two.
say.eli5: Each button jumps to a different part of the song.

steps.q: What is a hot cue?
options: a saved spot you can jump to instantly
steps.why: Press it and the track jumps there.

whyWrong.1: It's about position, not sound.
whyWrong.3: Effects change the sound.

steps.q: What does halving a loop again and again do?
options: builds tension as it repeats faster
steps.why: Four bars, two, one, a beat. The urgency climbs.

whyWrong.1: The tempo stays the same.
whyWrong.3: You let go and it carries on.

steps.q: What is cue juggling?
options: flicking between two cues for a stutter
steps.why: Back and forth between two saved spots makes a rhythm.

whyWrong.1: It's about playing them, not setting them.
whyWrong.2: It's done on the cue buttons.
whyWrong.3: Nothing to do with drives.

steps.next: Back to the song path: reading waveforms.

lessons.title: energy management

song.why: where your song goes in a set depends on whether it builds, holds or releases the energy

lessons.learn: Building, holding and releasing energy across a set, and deciding what job your song does in that arc.
youCan: say how djs build and release energy
decide what job your song does in a set
blend toward more or less energy

say.mentor: Two grooves. One could lift a room, the other could let it breathe. Managing energy is choosing which comes next: when to push, when to hold, when to let the crowd exhale.
say.straight: Energy management is choosing when to push, when to hold and when to release.
say.eli5: Some songs make people jump. Some let them rest. Djs choose which one comes next.

say.mentor:
To build, raise the intensity over several tracks: a little faster, busier, harder. To hold, stay on a plateau for a few tracks at the top. To release, drop to a lighter track or a breakdown and let the crowd breathe.
Long sets have several peaks and valleys, not one long peak. The valleys are what make the peaks feel high. Done well, nobody notices you're doing it. The crowd just can't stop dancing.
say.straight: Build over several tracks, hold at the top, release with something lighter. Several peaks and valleys beat one long peak.
say.eli5: Go up a bit at a time, stay up for a while, then come down to rest. Then go up again.

deeper.title: the double drop
deeper.say: A double drop is two tracks hitting their drops at the same moment, both basses and both sets of drums at once. Rare, risky, and huge when it works.

say.mentor:
Is your song a builder, a peak or a release? Decide. Then pick deck b to do the next job: a track that pushes the energy on from your song, or one that lets it settle.
Bring deck b in, swap the bass with the low knobs, and take your song out. Listen to where the room would go.
say.straight: Decide your song's job: build, peak or release. Pick deck b for the next job. Fader b up, low a down, then crossfade to b or pull deck a down.
say.eli5: Is your song for jumping or resting? Pick the next song. Push it up, turn your song's low knob down, then slide over.

steps.q: Why have valleys in a set?
options: they make the peaks feel higher
to give the dj a rest
steps.why: Contrast. A peak only feels high next to something lower.

whyWrong.1: They're for the crowd, not you.
whyWrong.3: Genre can stay the same.

steps.q: How do you build energy?
options: raise the intensity over several tracks
steps.why: Step by step, a little faster or harder each time.

whyWrong.1: Then you have nowhere to go.
whyWrong.3: Silence drops it.

steps.q: What is a double drop?
options: two tracks hitting their drops together
steps.why: Both drops at the same moment, both basses, both drums.

whyWrong.1: It's two different tracks.
whyWrong.3: One dj, two tracks.

steps.next: Back to the song path: effects in performance.

lessons.title: genre strategy

song.why: your song has a sound, and the set you build around it says who you are as a dj

lessons.learn: Knowing your sound, playing to the room, and building a short set around your own song's genre.
youCan: describe your sound in tempo and style
pick tracks that sit around your song
say how to widen your sound without losing it

say.mentor: A house groove at 124. A dj known for this sound gets booked for the nights that want it. That's your sound: the genres, the tempo range and the energy people know you for.
say.straight: Your sound is the genres, tempo range and energy you're known for. It's what gets you booked.
say.eli5: Every dj has a kind of music they're known for. That's their sound.

say.mentor:
Some djs are specialists, deep in one genre. Others are eclectic and range across many. Either works if it's clearly you, because promoters book the sound they can count on.
Widen it slowly, into neighbouring genres: deep house to tech house to techno, not house to drum and bass overnight. And let the venue set the range. A warehouse techno night isn't a beach bar.
Above all, play music you love. A crowd can hear when you mean it.
say.straight: Specialist or eclectic, be clearly you. Widen into neighbouring genres slowly. Fit the venue. Play what you love.
say.eli5: Play the music you love most. Add new kinds slowly. Think about where you're playing.

say.mentor:
Build a tiny set around your song. Look at its bpm on deck a and think about which genre it sits in.
Then tap through the bank and keep the tracks that belong in the same world: close in tempo on their chips, and a groove that sits with yours when you play them against your song. Three that belong is a set with a sound.
say.straight: Find your song's genre from its bpm. Tap through the bank and keep three tracks that sit with it in tempo and groove.
say.eli5: Listen to each other song with yours. Keep three that feel like they belong together.

steps.q: Why does a clear sound help a dj get booked?
steps.why: A promoter books the sound they can count on.

whyWrong.1: It usually means the right bookings.
whyWrong.2: Beatmatching is the same either way.
whyWrong.3: It's not a rule.

steps.q: How should you widen your sound?
steps.why: Neighbouring genres keep it sounding like you.

whyWrong.1: Big jumps lose your identity.
whyWrong.2: Then nobody knows what to expect.
whyWrong.3: Sounds grow as taste grows.

steps.q: What is a specialist dj?
options: one who goes deep in one genre
steps.why: Depth in one niche.

whyWrong.1: Gear doesn't make a specialist.
whyWrong.3: Format isn't the point.

steps.next: Back to the song path: effects in performance.

lessons.title: effects, deep

song.why: an echo out of your song carries its last beat across into the next track

lessons.learn: Choosing effects on purpose: echo size, the reverb wash, flanger and phaser, and an echo out from your song into the next track.
youCan: do an echo out of your song
say how echo size changes the feel
describe a reverb wash

say.mentor: Kick and clap. Imagine that last clap repeating, quieter each time, as the next track comes in. That's echo used on purpose. Going deeper with effects doesn't mean using more of them. It means choosing each one for what it does to the moment.
say.straight: Deeper effects work is choosing each effect for the moment, not using more.
say.eli5: Imagine the last clap repeating and getting quieter. Djs choose effects like that on purpose.

say.mentor:
Echo size matters. A half beat echo flutters fast. A one bar echo leaves long gaps between repeats.
A reverb wash turns the reverb's feedback up so it swells, then cuts the dry track (the track without the effect), leaving only the cloud. A flanger sweeps like a jet plane, strong on hats and snares. A phaser moves more slowly and adds depth to pads.
The hardest skill is not using them. One effect at the right moment is a memory. Effects on every blend are noise.
say.straight: Half beat echo flutters, one bar echo leaves gaps. Reverb wash: feedback up, dry track cut. Flanger: jet plane sweep. Phaser: slower depth. Use them rarely.
say.eli5: Short echoes flutter fast, long echoes wait between repeats. Some effects swoosh like a plane. Use them only sometimes.

say.mentor:
Both decks are playing and matched, with the crossfader on your song. Turn deck a's echo up and let your song's last beats start to repeat.
Then crossfade to b while the echo rings. Your song echoes away under the new track.
say.straight: Echo a up, then crossfade to b while the echo rings.
say.eli5: Turn up the echo on your song. Then slide the big slider over to b.

steps.q: What changes between a half beat echo and a one bar echo?
steps.why: Shorter size, faster repeats.

whyWrong.1: Echo doesn't change key.
whyWrong.3: They feel very different.

steps.q: What is a reverb wash?
options: the reverb swells up, then the dry track is cut
a short reverb with no tail
reverb on the new track only
steps.why: Only the reverb cloud is left, fading away.

whyWrong.1: A wash is all tail.
whyWrong.3: Eq shapes frequencies.

steps.q: What's the advanced skill with effects?
options: knowing when not to use them
using as many as possible at once
steps.why: Restraint makes the moments count.

whyWrong.1: Then they stop meaning anything.
whyWrong.3: Presets are fine. Choosing is the skill.

steps.next: Back to the song path: preparing a set.

lessons.title: stem djing

song.why: splitting tracks into parts lets your song and another track share one groove

lessons.learn: What stems are, mixing parts of tracks instead of whole tracks, and a rough version of it with the eq on your song.
youCan: say what a stem is
say why stems are never perfectly clean
split two tracks by frequency with the eq

say.mentor: Two whole tracks. Normally a dj mixes them whole. Stems change that. Software splits a track into its parts, such as drums, bass, melody and vocals, and gives each part its own level. Then you mix parts, not tracks.
say.straight: Stems are the separate parts of a track, like drums, bass, melody and vocals. Stem djing mixes parts, not whole tracks.
say.eli5: A computer can pull a song apart into drums, bass, tune and singing. Then you can mix just the parts you want.

say.mentor:
Keep the drums of both tracks running while you swap the bass and the melody. Or run your song's drums under another track's vocal. The beat never breaks.
The split is done by machine learning, and it isn't perfect. On busy tracks a bit of one part leaks into another, so a drums only stem can still carry a ghost of the bass.
say.straight: Keep both drums while swapping bass and melody, or put one track's drums under another's vocal. Machine learning does the split, and parts can leak.
say.eli5: You can keep the drums going while swapping the rest. The computer isn't perfect, so bits sometimes sneak into the wrong part.

say.mentor:
Stems split a track into its parts. Deck b's parts are drums, hats and bass, each with its own button. Take deck b's drums out and bring its fader up.
Now you've got deck b's bass line playing under your song's drums: two tracks combined part by part, which no eq can do as cleanly. Try taking the hats out too, or the bass instead.
say.straight: Deck b's drums, hats and bass are separate. Take its drums out and bring it up: its bass under your drums.
say.eli5: Each part of the song has its own button. Turn the drums off on one song.

steps.q: What is a stem?
options: one part of a track, like the drums or the vocal
steps.why: A separated part you can control on its own.

whyWrong.1: A stem is a piece of the track.
whyWrong.3: Playlists hold whole tracks.

steps.q: Why might a stem not be perfectly clean?
options: the machine learning split leaks between parts
steps.why: Busy productions are hard to pull apart perfectly.

whyWrong.1: Leaks are normal.
whyWrong.2: Drive speed doesn't affect the split.
whyWrong.3: Key has nothing to do with it.

steps.q: How is the eq different from stems?
options: it splits by frequency, not by instrument
steps.why: The low knob takes everything low, kick and bass together.

whyWrong.1: Stems separate instruments, the eq separates frequencies.
whyWrong.3: Key isn't involved.

steps.next: Back to the song path: preparing a set.

lessons.title: dvs and digital vinyl

song.why: with a timecode record, your song could be played and cut on a real turntable

lessons.learn: How timecode vinyl lets a turntable play digital files, who uses it, and the quick cut that comes from turntable culture, on your song.
youCan: say what a timecode record does
name the software a dvs setup runs
make a quick cut with the crossfader

say.mentor: Kick and clap, the kind of beat turntablists cut up. A digital vinyl system, dvs for short, lets them do it with digital files. A turntable plays a special record, and the software plays your track as if it were pressed on that vinyl.
say.straight: Dvs, a digital vinyl system, lets a turntable control digital files through a special record.
say.eli5: A dvs lets a dj use a real record player to play songs from a computer.

say.mentor:
The special record is timecode vinyl. Instead of music it carries a coded signal. The software reads that signal to know where the needle is and how fast the record is moving, then plays your file to match. Scratch the record and the file scratches.
You also need an audio interface that can read timecode. And expect needles and records to wear faster, because they're played all the time.
say.straight: Timecode vinyl carries a coded signal. Software reads needle position and speed from it and plays your file to match. Needs a timecode audio interface. Wears needles faster.
say.eli5: The record has a secret code instead of music. The computer listens to the code and plays your song at the same speed.

deeper.title: serato and traktor
deeper.say: Serato DJ Pro is the most common dvs software, especially in hip-hop and turntablism. Traktor Scratch Pro is Native Instruments' version.

say.mentor:
Hip-hop and turntablist djs live on the crossfader, so try their basic move. Deck b is matched and the crossfader is on your song.
Watch the counter and, on the one, snap the crossfader from a to b in one quick move. On a dvs rig it's the same move, with your song on a timecode record.
say.straight: On the one, snap the crossfader from a to b in one quick move.
say.eli5: When the counter says bar 1, whip the big slider from a to b.

steps.q: What does a timecode record carry?
options: a coded signal the software reads for position and speed
steps.why: The software turns that code into where the needle is and how fast it's moving.

whyWrong.1: The music is in your files.
whyWrong.2: The code is what makes it work.
whyWrong.3: Playlists live in the software.

steps.q: Who uses dvs most?
options: turntablists and vinyl djs with digital libraries
steps.why: It keeps the vinyl feel with digital music.

whyWrong.1: It's a club and battle tool.
whyWrong.3: It's for playing live.

steps.q: Why do needles wear faster with dvs?
options: the timecode records are played constantly
the records are made of glass
steps.why: Every track you play runs on the same record.

whyWrong.1: Volume isn't the issue.
whyWrong.3: They're ordinary vinyl.

steps.next: Back to the song path: recording your set.

lessons.title: the business of djing

song.why: a promoter books you on a mix and your own music, and your song is part of both

lessons.learn: What to send a promoter, setting a rate, the rider, and why being reliable gets you booked again.
youCan: say what goes to a promoter
say what a rider is
explain why reliability matters as much as talent

say.mentor: A clean blend between two tracks. Do that for an hour, record it, and you have the thing promoters ask for first: a promo mix. It's your audio cv, 60 to 90 minutes of your sound at its best.
say.straight: Promoters want a promo mix first: 60 to 90 minutes of your sound at its best.
say.eli5: People who run parties want to hear you first. So djs record a long mix to send them.

say.mentor:
Alongside the mix, have an artist name and look that are the same everywhere, and a steady presence where your audience listens, like Instagram, SoundCloud or Mixcloud. If you make music, send it too. Your own tracks are exclusives nobody else can play.
Know the local rates and don't undercut them. It devalues you and everyone else. A rider is your written list of what you need for the gig, technical and personal, agreed before the night.
Then be reliable. Turn up on time, prepared, and play what you promised. A promoter who can depend on you books you again.
say.straight: Send a promo mix and your own tracks. Keep one name and look everywhere. Know the rates and don't undercut. Agree a rider in advance. Be reliable.
say.eli5: Send your mix and your songs. Ask for fair pay. Write down what you need. Always turn up on time.

say.mentor:
A promo mix is this, done many times in a row. Play the handover that could open yours: your song on deck a, a bank track on deck b.
Bring deck b in, swap the bass with the low knobs, and take your song out. Make it clean enough that you'd send it.
say.straight: Play a handover you'd put in a promo mix. Fader b up, low a down, then crossfade to b or pull deck a down.
say.eli5: Mix your song into another one, as nicely as you can, like you're making a mix to send.

steps.q: What do promoters usually ask for first?
options: a promo mix of your sound
steps.why: It's how they hear whether your sound fits their night.

whyWrong.1: The venue usually has the gear.
whyWrong.2: Followers help, but the mix comes first.
whyWrong.3: Your mix is the cv.

steps.q: What is a rider?
options: a written list of your technical and personal needs for the gig
a dj who travels with you
a fee on top of your rate
steps.why: Agreed in writing before the night.

whyWrong.1: It's a document, not a person.
whyWrong.3: It's paperwork, not technique.

steps.q: What gets you booked again most reliably?
options: turning up prepared and on time
steps.why: Promoters rebook djs they can depend on.

whyWrong.1: Followers don't fix a no-show.
whyWrong.3: Reliability matters more than any track.

steps.next: Back to the song path: from dj to artist. Your own track in your set.

lessons.title: pulse and tempo

song.why: every song starts with a pulse, and yours starts with a kick you play in yourself, at a speed you choose

lessons.learn: The steady beat under every dance track, how fast it goes, and the first sound in your own song: a kick you play in and set to your own tempo.
youCan: feel the pulse of a track and count along with it
play a kick in on the beat
say what bpm means and roughly what speed house and techno sit at
set your song's tempo by ear

say.mentor:
Hear that thump? That's a kick drum, and it's playing the pulse: a steady beat that never speeds up or slows down. Every dance track you've ever moved to has one underneath it. It's the thing your foot taps to without asking.
Your song is going to start right here, with a pulse of your own.
say.straight: This is a kick drum playing the pulse: one hit on every beat, perfectly even. Every dance track is built on a pulse like this. Your song starts with one.
say.eli5:
Boom, boom, boom, boom. That's a kick drum. It's like a heartbeat for music: it goes at the same speed the whole time. When you tap your foot to a song, you're tapping to this.
Your song is going to start with a boom like this.

say.mentor:
Count with it, out loud if you can: one, two, three, four, then start again at one. Each kick is a beat. The pulse is just beats in a row.
Musicians count in fours almost all the time, because it's easy to feel and easy to dance to. You'll hear why that matters in the next lesson.
say.straight: Each kick is one beat. Count one to four and start again. Dance music almost always counts in fours.
say.eli5: Let's count the booms: one, two, three, four, and again, one, two, three, four. Every boom is called a beat. Musicians love counting to four.

say.mentor:
Now play the pulse yourself. This bar becomes the first thing in your song.
Press rec. You'll hear four clicks to count you in, so just listen. Then tap the kick pad once on each of the next four clicks. Any kick that lands early or late turns red, and you can play it again. Tap undo to take one back, hold it to start over.
say.straight: Record the pulse. Press rec, wait out four clicks, then tap the kick on each of the next four. Red means off the beat; undo takes one back, hold clears.
say.eli5: Your turn! Press the red rec button. Let four ticks go by, then tap the kick pad on every tick, four times. If a tap is too early or too late it goes red, so you can try that one again.

say.mentor:
That's your kick, looping. Now turn the knob and listen to what happens.
How fast the pulse goes is called the tempo, and it's counted in bpm: beats per minute. At 120 bpm there are two beats every second. Turn it down and everything feels heavier and lazier. Turn it up and it gets urgent. House usually lives around 120 to 128, techno a bit faster, garage and dubstep around 140.
Try the four speeds on the right, then pick the one that feels like your song. You can change it any time later.
say.straight: This is your kick at different speeds. Tempo is measured in bpm, beats per minute: 120 bpm is two beats a second. House sits around 120 to 128, techno a little higher, garage and dubstep near 140. Pick a tempo for your song.
say.eli5:
Turn the big knob and listen: your kick goes faster or slower. How fast the booms come is called the tempo. We count it in bpm, which means booms per minute. 120 bpm is two booms every second.
Slow feels sleepy and heavy. Fast feels exciting. Pick the speed you like best for your song.

steps.hint: The number is how many kicks you'd hear in one minute.

say.mentor:
So your song now has a pulse: a kick on every beat, at a tempo you chose. Everything you add from here lines up with it. The hats, the bass, the melody, all of it counts along with this kick.
Producers set the tempo first because changing it later changes how everything feels. A tune that's cheeky at 128 can sound sad at 100.
say.straight: Your song has a pulse and a tempo. Everything you add later is timed against it, which is why the tempo usually gets set first.
say.eli5: Now your song has a heartbeat, and you picked how fast it goes. Every sound you add later will dance along to it.

deeper.title: why 120 to 128 for house
deeper.say: It's close to a brisk walking pace, which is about as fast as people can dance to for hours without getting tired. Early Chicago house sat around 120. Techno from Detroit and Berlin pushed faster.

deeper.title: half time
deeper.say: Dubstep is 140 bpm, but it often feels like 70, because the big drums only hit on every other beat. The pulse is still 140 underneath. You'll hear the same trick in a lot of trap and drum and bass.

steps.q: What does bpm stand for?
steps.why: Beats per minute. 120 bpm means 120 beats, 120 kicks here, in one minute.

whyWrong.1: A bar is a group of beats. Tempo counts the beats themselves.
whyWrong.2: Close, but it's per minute. That's what makes it a speed.
whyWrong.3: It's beats, the steady pulse you counted along with.

steps.q: At 120 bpm, how many beats happen every second?
steps.why: 120 beats in 60 seconds is two every second.

whyWrong.1: One a second would be 60 bpm, half your song's speed.
whyWrong.2: Four a second would be 240 bpm, far faster than any house track.
whyWrong.3: Twelve a second would be a buzz, not a beat.

steps.q: You turn the tempo from 120 up to 140. What happens to your kick?
options: the kick gets higher in pitch
you get more kicks in each bar
steps.why: Same pattern, played faster. Each beat is shorter, so the kicks arrive sooner.

whyWrong.1: Tempo changes speed, not volume.
whyWrong.2: The kick sounds the same, it just comes round more often.
whyWrong.3: Still one kick per beat. There are just more beats in each minute.

steps.q: Roughly what tempo does house music usually sit at?
steps.why: House usually sits between 120 and 128. Techno goes a little faster.

whyWrong.1: That's ballad speed, slower than most dance music.
whyWrong.3: That's faster than almost any dance floor.

steps.q: Why does the click play while you record?
options: so you have something to play along to
it becomes part of your song
to count how many kicks you played
steps.why: The click is a guide to keep you on the beat. It never goes into your song.

whyWrong.1: The click stays out of your song. Only your kicks go in.
whyWrong.2: It doesn't touch the kick at all.
whyWrong.3: It just ticks on every beat.

steps.q: At 60 bpm, how long is one beat?
steps.why: 60 beats in 60 seconds, so one beat every second.

whyWrong.1: Half a second is a beat at 120 bpm.
whyWrong.2: Two seconds a beat would be 30 bpm.
whyWrong.3: That would be 600 bpm.

steps.q: Why do producers usually set the tempo first?
options: changing it later changes how everything feels
the kick only works at one tempo
bpm sets how loud the song is
steps.why: Every part is played against the pulse. Change the speed and the whole mood shifts with it.

whyWrong.1: You can change it any time. It just changes the feel of everything already there.
whyWrong.2: A kick works at any tempo.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is speed, not loudness.

steps.q: Dubstep is 140 bpm but often feels like 70. Why?
options: the big drums hit on every other beat
the bass is out of time
steps.why: Half time. The pulse is still 140, but the heavy drums skip every other beat, so it feels half as fast.

whyWrong.1: Clubs play it at 140.
whyWrong.2: The bass is right on the grid, it just leaves space.
whyWrong.3: There's always a pulse underneath.

steps.next: Next: bars and counting. A clap on two and four turns your pulse into a groove, and your loop grows to four bars.

lessons.title: bars and counting

song.why: a clap on two and four turns a pulse into a groove you can dance to

lessons.learn: How musicians count, what a bar is, and the clap on two and four that turns your kick into a groove.
youCan: count bars of four along with a track
hear the backbeat, the clap on two and four
play a clap in on two and four over your kick
read 4/4 and know what it means

say.mentor:
Same steady kick as before, with one thing added: a clap on every other beat. Listen to how much that changes. The kick on its own just marches. With the clap it starts to swing back and forth, and your head wants to nod.
That clap is called the backbeat, and it's in almost every song you know.
say.straight: A kick on every beat, plus a clap on every other beat. That clap is the backbeat. It's what turns a pulse into a groove.
say.eli5: Boom, clap, boom, clap. Hear how the clap makes it bouncier? The boom is the kick you already know. The clap comes in between, on every other beat. It makes you want to nod your head.

say.mentor:
Count along again: one, two, three, four. Notice where the clap lands: on two and on four, never on one or three. One and three are the kick on its own. Two and four get the clap.
Those four beats together are called a bar. Musicians count music in bars, the way you'd count a walk in steps: "the bass comes in after eight bars". Dance music is almost always four beats to a bar, written 4/4 and said "four four".
say.straight: Four beats make a bar. The clap lands on beats two and four of every bar. Dance music is nearly always in 4/4: four beats per bar.
say.eli5:
Count with it: one, two, three, four. The clap comes on two and on four. One and three are just the boom.
Four beats in a row make a bar, like four steps make a little walk. Most dance music counts to four and starts again.

deeper.title: what 4/4 means
deeper.say: The top four is how many beats are in a bar. The bottom four says each beat is a quarter note, the usual size of a beat. You'll see it at the start of sheet music and in your Live set's tempo box.

deeper.title: other counts
deeper.say: A waltz counts in three, 3/4: one two three, one two three. Some music counts in five or seven. You'll find them in jazz, prog and film scores. Clubs stick to four because four is easiest to dance to for a long time.

say.mentor:
Now add the clap to your song, over the kick you played last time.
Press rec, let the four clicks count you in, then tap the clap pad on two and on four: skip one, clap on two, skip three, clap on four. A clap on the wrong beat turns red so you can play it again. Undo takes one back, hold it to start over.
say.straight: Record the backbeat over your kick. Rec, wait out the count-in, then clap on two and four. Red means off the beat.
say.eli5: Your turn! Press rec and wait for four ticks. Then count one, two, three, four, and tap the clap pad only on two and four. Skip one, clap, skip three, clap.

steps.hint: One and three are the kick on its own. Clap in between them.

say.mentor:
That's your first groove: kick on every beat, clap on two and four. The clap on two and four is the backbeat, and it's one of the oldest tricks in pop music.
It works because it pulls against the kick. The kick says "down", the clap says "up", and your body sits in between, nodding. Next time you hear a song, find two and four. You'll hear a clap or a snare there almost every time.
say.straight: Kick on every beat, clap on two and four: that's the backbeat. The kick gives the down, the clap the up, and that back and forth is the groove.
say.eli5: Now your song goes boom, clap, boom, clap. That clap on two and four has a name: the backbeat. Almost every song has one. See if you can spot it in the next song you hear.

deeper.title: where the backbeat comes from
deeper.say: Rhythm and blues and early rock and roll drummers hit the snare hard on two and four in the 1940s and 50s, and pop never let it go. Disco kept it, house swapped the snare for a drum machine clap, and here we are.

deeper.title: clap or snare
deeper.say: House and techno often use a clap, hip hop and rock a snare, and plenty of tracks use both at once. You'll compare them properly in the producer world.

steps.q: How many beats are in one bar of dance music?
steps.why: Dance music is almost always 4/4, four beats to a bar.

whyWrong.1: Two beats is half a bar. Count along again and listen for the clap on two and four.
whyWrong.3: Three to a bar is a waltz, not a club track.

steps.q: Which beats does the backbeat clap land on?
steps.why: Two and four. One and three are the kick on its own.

whyWrong.1: One and three are where the kick sits alone. The clap answers it on two and four.
whyWrong.2: Every beat is the kick's job. The clap is on every other one.
whyWrong.3: One is the start of the bar, where the kick lands.

steps.q: What does 4/4 mean?
steps.why: The top four is the number of beats in a bar.

whyWrong.1: Songs have far more than four bars. It's about the beats inside one bar.
whyWrong.2: It's about counting time, not how many sounds play.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is written in bpm. 4/4 is how the beats are grouped.

steps.q: A producer says "the bass comes in after eight bars". At 120 bpm, roughly how long is that?
steps.why: At 120 bpm a bar of four beats lasts two seconds, so eight bars is sixteen seconds.

whyWrong.1: That would be one second a bar, too fast at 120.
whyWrong.3: A minute at 120 is thirty bars.

steps.q: Why does adding a clap on two and four make the beat feel groovier?
options: it pulls against the kick, so the beat goes down and up
steps.why: The kick says down, the clap says up. That back and forth is what makes you nod.

whyWrong.1: The tempo stays the same. Only the pattern changes.
whyWrong.3: A clap has no tune to it.

steps.q: A waltz counts one two three, one two three. How is that written?
steps.why: Three beats to a bar, each one a quarter note.

whyWrong.1: 4/4 is four beats to a bar, like dance music.
whyWrong.2: The bottom number is the size of a beat, usually four.
whyWrong.3: That would mean one beat to a bar.

steps.next: Next: subdivision. Hats on the eighths and sixteenths fill the space between your kicks, and snap shows up to help you place them.

lessons.title: subdivision

song.why: hats fill the space between your kicks, and how finely you split the beat sets how busy the groove feels

lessons.learn: Splitting the beat into halves and quarters, eighths and sixteenths, and a hat pattern in your song that uses them. This is also where snap comes in.
youCan: hear the difference between quarters, eighths and sixteenths
play hats on the eighths or sixteenths with snap on
say what snap does and when to turn it off

say.mentor:
Tap through the three. Same kick each time, but the hats split each beat differently.
Quarters: one hat per beat, right on the kick. Eighths: two per beat, one on the kick and one exactly halfway to the next. Sixteenths: four per beat, a fast tick-tick-tick-tick. Listen to how the groove gets busier and faster-feeling while the tempo stays exactly the same.
say.straight: Three ways to split the beat with a hi hat: quarters (one per beat), eighths (two), sixteenths (four). The tempo never changes, only how finely the beat is cut.
say.eli5: Tap a, b and c. The boom stays the same. The tiny tss sound changes. One tss per boom, then two, then four really quick ones. More tss makes it feel busier, but the song isn't going any faster.

steps.title: halves and quarters of a beat

say.mentor:
Musicians call these note values. A quarter note is one beat. An eighth note is half a beat. A sixteenth is a quarter of a beat. The names come from how many fit in a bar: four quarters, eight eighths, sixteen sixteenths.
People count eighths as "one and two and three and four and", and sixteenths as "one e and a, two e and a". Say it out loud over the sixteenths and you'll hear it lock in.
say.straight: Quarter note: one beat. Eighth: half a beat. Sixteenth: a quarter of a beat. Count eighths as "one and two and", sixteenths as "one e and a".
say.eli5: Grown-up musicians give these names. One tss per boom is a quarter note. Two per boom is an eighth note. Four per boom is a sixteenth note. You can count the fast ones as "one e and a, two e and a".

deeper.title: why the names are fractions
deeper.say: A bar of 4/4 holds one whole note. Cut it in four and you get quarter notes, in eight and you get eighths, in sixteen and you get sixteenths. Sheet music draws each one differently, but in a producer's grid they're just the lines getting closer together.

say.mentor:
Now put hats in your song. Hats on the eighths between your kicks are the classic house sound.
This time you get help: snap. Snap moves every hit to the nearest line on the grid, so a hat that's a hair early still lands exactly on the eighth. It's set to eighths. Tap the snap key to change it to sixteenths or turn it off and hear the difference.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and tap the hat between the kicks: on every "and".
say.straight: Record hats over your beat. Snap is on, set to eighths, so every hit lands on the nearest eighth. Tap the snap key to try sixteenths or off. Rec, count-in, then tap the hat on every "and".
say.eli5: Your turn to add the tss. A helper called snap is switched on: it nudges every tap onto the nearest line, so it always sounds neat. Press rec, wait for four ticks, then tap the hat in between the booms.

steps.hint: Say "one and two and" and tap on every "and".

say.mentor:
That's snap, also called quantise. Almost every music program has it. It's brilliant for drums that need to be tight, like hats and kicks in a club track.
But it's not always what you want. A little looseness is what makes a groove feel human. Producers often play something in, snap it, then nudge a few hits back off the grid on purpose. You'll do that in the swing lesson next.
say.straight: Snap (quantise) moves hits to the nearest grid line. Use it for tight drums; turn it off or loosen it when you want a human feel.
say.eli5: Snap is like a magnet that pulls your taps onto the lines. Great for neat drums. Sometimes you want a bit of wobble so it feels more alive, and then you switch the magnet off.

steps.q: How many sixteenth notes fit in one beat?
steps.why: A sixteenth is a quarter of a beat, so four fit in one beat and sixteen in a bar.

whyWrong.1: Two per beat is eighths.
whyWrong.2: Sixteen fit in a whole bar of four beats.
whyWrong.3: Eight per beat would be thirty-second notes.

steps.q: You switch your hats from eighths to sixteenths. What happens to the tempo?
steps.why: The pulse doesn't change. The beat is just cut into smaller pieces, so it feels busier.

whyWrong.1: The kick keeps the same speed. Only the hats get busier.
whyWrong.2: Nothing slows down. There are just more hats in each beat.
whyWrong.3: Tempo only changes when you turn the tempo knob.

steps.q: What does snap do to a hit that's slightly early?
options: moves it to the nearest grid line
moves it to the start of the bar
steps.why: Snap pulls each hit onto the nearest line of the grid it's set to.

whyWrong.1: Snap never removes notes.
whyWrong.2: It moves notes in time, it doesn't touch their volume.
whyWrong.3: Only to the nearest line, not all the way back to one.

steps.q: How do musicians count eighth notes?
options: one and two and three and four and
steps.why: Each beat plus an "and" halfway through.

whyWrong.1: One e and a is sixteenths, four per beat.
whyWrong.3: That's counting in twos, not eighths.

steps.q: Why might a producer turn snap off?
options: to keep a looser, more human feel
because snap only works on kicks
steps.why: Perfectly gridded drums can sound stiff. A few hits off the grid feel played by a person.

whyWrong.1: Snap has nothing to do with tempo.
whyWrong.3: Snap moves timing, not volume.

steps.next: Next: groove and swing. Push every other sixteenth a little late and your hats start to bounce.

lessons.title: groove and swing

song.why: swing pushes every other sixteenth a little late, and your beat starts to bounce instead of march

lessons.learn: What swing is, why it makes people move, and a swing setting for your whole song.
youCan: hear the difference between straight and swung
say which notes swing moves and which it leaves alone
set the swing on your song by ear

say.mentor: Tap straight, then swung. Same kick, same clap, same hats. In the swung one, every other hat is pushed a little late, and suddenly it bounces. That's swing, and it's the difference between a beat that marches and a beat that grooves.
say.straight: Straight vs swung. The swung version delays every other sixteenth a little. That small delay is what gives it a bounce.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. In b, every second tss is a tiny bit late, like a skip in your step. Hear how it bounces now? That's called swing.

say.mentor:
Here's your own song with a swing knob on it. Turn it up and listen to your hats.
Swing only moves the off sixteenths: the "e" and the "a" in "one e and a". The beats and the "ands" stay exactly where they are, so your kick and clap don't move. At about 50 percent the off notes land a third of the way along, a triplet feel. House producers often sit somewhere between 10 and 30 percent. Push it to the top for a heavy shuffle.
Pick the amount that makes you want to move.
say.straight: Swing delays only the off sixteenths. Kick, clap and eighths stay put. Around 50 percent is a triplet feel, house usually sits lower. Set the amount for your song.
say.eli5: Turn the swing knob and listen to your song. More swing makes the in-between tss sounds later and bouncier. Your boom and clap stay right where they are. Stop when it makes you want to dance.

steps.hint: If your hats are only on the eighths, swing won't move them. It needs sixteenths to bite.

say.mentor:
People don't play exactly on a grid. A drummer leans on some notes and lags others, and our ears hear that as feel. Swing is a simple way to get some of that back into programmed music.
Swing in drum machines goes back to Roger Linn's machines and the Akai MPC, the tool behind a lot of hip hop and house. Producers still talk about "MPC swing" as a sound of its own.
say.straight: Real players never sit exactly on the grid. Swing puts a little of that feel back. The MPC made it famous in hip hop and house.
say.eli5: When people play drums, they're never perfectly exact, and that wobble feels good. Swing adds a little wobble on purpose.

deeper.title: swing in tracks you know
deeper.say: Listen to almost any J Dilla beat for heavy, loose swing, or to UK garage, where swung hats and shuffled snares are the whole sound. A lot of deep house has gentle swing you only notice when it's gone.

steps.q: Which notes does swing move?
options: the off sixteenths, the e and the a
the first beat of every bar
steps.why: Swing pushes the off sixteenths late. The beats and the ands stay put.

whyWrong.1: If every note moved the same amount, nothing would sound different.
whyWrong.2: The kick on the beat doesn't move.
whyWrong.3: Beat one stays exactly where it is.

steps.q: Your hats are only on the eighths. You turn swing up. What happens?
steps.why: Eighths are on the beat or the and, which swing leaves alone. Add sixteenths to hear it.

whyWrong.1: Swing changes timing, not volume.
whyWrong.2: Swing only ever pushes notes late.
whyWrong.3: Tempo stays the same.

steps.q: About how much swing gives a triplet feel?
steps.why: At around 50 percent the off notes land a third of the way along, like a triplet.

whyWrong.1: Zero is straight, no swing at all.
whyWrong.2: 5 percent is a hint you can barely hear.
whyWrong.3: The knob tops out before that.

steps.q: Why does swing make a beat feel more human?
options: real players don't sit exactly on the grid
steps.why: People lean on and lag notes. Swing puts back some of that feel.

whyWrong.1: Swing changes timing only.
whyWrong.2: Nothing new is added, only moved.
whyWrong.3: The tempo is the same.

steps.next: Next: what sound actually is, and the first notes of your melody, played over your beat.

lessons.title: what is sound?

song.why: your first sound in your song, a few notes you play yourself

lessons.learn: What sound actually is, the three things every sound has, and the first few notes of your own song.
youCan: explain sound as air being pushed and pulled
tell pitch from loudness
hear how the shape of a wave changes its colour
play your first notes into your song

say.mentor:
Everything you will ever hear, a kick, a voice, a whole song, is the same thing underneath: air being pushed and pulled.
Watch the picture while the note plays. The speaker cone moves out and in, fast. Moving out, it shoves the air in front of it together. Moving in, it leaves the air spread thin. Those bunched and thin patches roll through the room to your ear, and your ear turns them into sound.
say.straight:
All sound works the same way: something moves back and forth and pushes the air around it.
In the picture, the speaker moves out and in. Out squeezes the air, in lets it spread. Those squeezed and spread patches travel to your ear, which hears them as sound.
say.eli5:
Hear that hum? Watch the speaker on the left. It wiggles out and in, really fast.
Each wiggle pushes the air, like ripples when you drop a stone in water. The ripples travel across the room into your ear, and that is what you hear. Sound is just wiggling air.

deeper.title: how fast sound travels
deeper.say: Those pressure patches move at about 343 metres every second in air. That is why you see lightning before you hear thunder: light is far faster.

say.mentor:
Every sound has three things. The first is pitch. Tap low, then high.
One full push and pull of the air is called a cycle. Pitch is how many cycles happen every second. The low note pushes the air about 110 times a second, the high one about 440. Look at the wave: more cycles packed in means a higher note. We count cycles per second in hertz, written Hz.
say.straight:
Thing one: pitch. Low, then high.
Pitch is how many push and pull cycles happen per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Here the low note is about 110 Hz and the high one about 440 Hz. More cycles in the picture, higher note.
say.eli5:
Every sound has three things. Number one is pitch. Tap low, then tap high.
A low note wiggles the air slowly. A high note wiggles it fast. In the picture the high one has lots of wiggles packed close together. More wiggles every second, higher note.

deeper.title: what people can hear
deeper.say: From about 20 cycles a second, a rumble you feel more than hear, up to about 20,000, a faint hiss. A kick drum sits around 50. The A a band tunes to is 440.

say.mentor:
The second thing is loudness. Tap quiet, then loud.
Same note, same pitch. What changes is how hard the air is pushed. The picture shows it as how tall the wave is: a small push makes a short wave and a quiet sound, a big push makes a tall wave and a loud one. Pitch is how often, loudness is how hard.
say.straight:
Thing two: loudness. Quiet, then loud.
The pitch stays the same. The size of the push changes, which shows as the height of the wave. How often is pitch, how hard is loudness.
say.eli5:
Number two is loudness. Tap quiet, then tap loud.
It is the same note. The loud one just pushes the air harder, so the wave in the picture is taller. Gentle push, quiet. Big push, loud.

say.mentor:
The third thing is the shape of the wave, and this is what makes a piano sound different from a guitar playing the same note. Tap soft, saw and square.
All three have the same pitch and loudness. Only the shape changes. The round wave sounds pure and gentle. The saw, a slope then a sudden drop, sounds bright and buzzy. The square sounds hollow, a bit like an old video game. People call this the colour, or timbre, of a sound.
say.straight:
Thing three: the shape of the wave, also called timbre or tone colour. Switch between soft, saw and square.
Same pitch, same loudness, different shape: pure, bright and buzzy, hollow. That is why two instruments playing the same note still sound different.
say.eli5:
Number three is the shape of the wiggle. Tap soft, saw and square.
Same note, same loudness, but they sound different. The soft one hums. The saw buzzes like a bee. The square sounds like an old video game. That shape is why a piano and a guitar never sound the same.

deeper.title: why the shape changes the sound
deeper.say: A smooth wave is just the one pitch. Sharp corners and sudden jumps add lots of extra, higher pitches on top, quietly. Your ear hears that mix as brightness or buzz.

say.mentor:
Now make some sound of your own. These are the first notes of your song, and every lesson after this adds something to it.
Press rec, let the four clicks go by, then play any four or more keys. Every key here fits with the others, so nothing you press can sound wrong. Listen to the pitch go up as you move right.
say.straight: Your first notes, recorded into your song. Press rec, wait out the count-in, then play at least four keys. They are all from one scale, so they all work together.
say.eli5:
Your turn to make sound! Whatever you play goes into your song.
Press rec, wait for four clicks, then press some keys. Any keys. They all sound nice together. Keys on the right are higher, keys on the left are lower.

steps.q: What is sound?
steps.why: Something moves back and forth and pushes the air. Those pressure changes reach your ear as sound.

whyWrong.1: Electricity drives the speaker, but what you hear is the air the speaker moves.
whyWrong.2: Light is a different thing. Sound travels through air.
whyWrong.3: Sound is movement of air, not heat.

steps.q: The high note had more wiggles packed into the picture. What does that mean?
options: the air moves back and forth faster
steps.why: More cycles every second means faster vibration, and that is a higher pitch.

whyWrong.1: Loudness is how hard the air is pushed, not how often.
whyWrong.2: Both notes were the same soft shape. Only the speed changed.
whyWrong.3: Both lasted the same time.

steps.q: What changed between the quiet note and the loud note?
options: how hard the air was pushed
how fast the air moved back and forth
steps.why: Same pitch, bigger push. A taller wave is a louder sound.

whyWrong.1: That would change the pitch. Both notes were the same pitch.
whyWrong.2: Both were the same soft shape.
whyWrong.3: Tap them again. The loud one pushes the air much harder.

steps.q: A piano and a guitar play the same note. Why do they still sound different?
options: the shape of their waves is different
steps.why: Same pitch, different wave shape. That shape is the sound's colour, or timbre.

whyWrong.1: Play them at the same loudness and they still sound different.
whyWrong.2: The question says same note, so the pitch is the same.
whyWrong.3: You heard soft, saw and square sound different on the same note.

steps.q: Which three things does every sound have?
steps.why: How often the air moves (pitch), how hard (loudness) and the shape of each cycle (timbre).

whyWrong.1: Close in spirit, but the three are pitch, loudness and wave shape.
whyWrong.2: Those are parts of the pitch range.
whyWrong.3: Those are about rhythm and music, not about a single sound.

steps.next: Next: frequency and pitch, up close. How notes are named and why some sound good together.

lessons.title: frequency and pitch

song.why: a tune for your song, played on keys that now have names

lessons.learn: Why a high note is high, what a note's name means, and the one rule that makes an octave: twice the speed, same name. Then a short tune of your own.
youCan: say what frequency is and what hertz counts
name the notes a to g and find the same note an octave up
explain why an octave sounds like the same note, higher
play a tune using low and high versions of the same note

say.mentor:
Tap a, then tap the one above it. The second note sounds like the same note, just higher. That is not an accident. It is the one rule that pitch is built on.
A note is the air wiggling back and forth. How fast it wiggles is its frequency, counted in hertz: wiggles per second. The first a wiggles 220 times a second. The second one wiggles 440 times a second, exactly twice as fast. Look at the picture: twice as many waves fit in the same window. Double the speed and you get the same note again, one octave up.
say.straight:
Tap both. The second is the first one, an octave up.
Pitch is frequency: how many times a second the air moves back and forth, measured in hertz. This a is 220 hz. The a above it is 440 hz, double. Doubling the frequency gives you the same note name one octave higher, which is why the picture shows twice as many waves.
say.eli5:
Tap the first button, then the second. Hear how the second one is the same but higher? Like a grown up and a kid singing the same thing.
Sound is air wiggling. Fast wiggles make high notes, slow wiggles make low notes. The first note wiggles 220 times every second. The second one wiggles 440 times, that is two times faster. Two times faster always gives you the same note, just higher up.

deeper.title: what hertz means
deeper.say: One hertz is one wiggle per second. It is named after Heinrich Hertz, who studied waves in the 1880s. People can hear from about 20 hz, a deep rumble, up to about 20,000 hz, a thin whistle. Most of music sits between 30 hz and 5,000 hz.

deeper.title: the kick and the bass are low frequencies
deeper.say: Your kick's body hums at around 50 hz. A bass line lives between about 40 hz and 200 hz. That is why they are the sounds you feel in your chest: slow, big pushes of air.

say.mentor:
Musicians do not say "440 hertz". They say a. Every pitch has a letter name: a, b, c, d, e, f, g. After g the names start again at a, one octave up. So the a at 440 hz and the a at 220 hz share a name because one is exactly double the other.
The keys you are about to play are labelled with these names. The first key and the last key are both a, an octave apart. The ones between are the notes that fit nicely with a, which is why anything you play on them sounds like it belongs together.
say.straight:
Pitches get letter names, a to g, then the letters repeat an octave higher. Two notes with the same name are a doubling apart: 110, 220, 440, 880 are all a.
The keys in this lesson are labelled. First and last are both a, one octave apart, and the six in between are from a scale that fits with a. More on scales in a later lesson.
say.eli5:
Notes have names, like people. The names are letters: a, b, c, d, e, f, g. After g you get a again, just higher. So a low a and a high a are a bit like a big cat and a kitten with the same name.
The keys you are going to press have their names written on them. The first key is a. The last key is also a, but higher.

deeper.title: why 440
deeper.say: Orchestras tune to the a at 440 hz. That has been the agreed standard since the 1950s, so a piano in Bengaluru and one in Berlin play the same a. Before that, a drifted between about 415 and 460 hz depending on the city.

deeper.title: the notes in between
deeper.say: Between one a and the next there are actually twelve steps, not seven. The five extra ones are the black keys on a piano: a sharp, c sharp, d sharp, f sharp, g sharp. You will meet them when scales come up. For now the seven letters are enough.

deeper.title: bpm and hz are not the same
deeper.say: Your song runs at 120 bpm, beats per minute: two beats a second. The low a is 220 hz, wiggles per second. Different things, both measured as how often something happens.

say.mentor:
Now use the octave in your song. This tune replaces the notes you played in the last lesson.
Press rec and let the four clicks go by. Play the first key, a. Then the last key, the a an octave up. Then two more keys you like. Listen for the jump between the two a's: same note, higher.
say.straight:
Record a short tune for your song. It replaces last lesson's notes.
Rec, wait out the count-in, play the low a (first key), the high a (last key), then any two more. At least four notes.
say.eli5:
Your turn. This tune goes into your song.
Press rec, wait for four clicks. Press the first key. Press the last key. Those are both a, low and high. Then press two more keys you like.

steps.q: A higher note means the air is wiggling
steps.why: Pitch is frequency. More wiggles a second, higher note. The a above went from 220 to 440 a second.

whyWrong.1: Slower wiggles make lower notes. The high a wiggled twice as fast as the low one.
whyWrong.2: How hard the air is pushed is loudness, not pitch. That was the last lesson.
whyWrong.3: How long a note lasts does not change its pitch. The a was high from the first instant.

steps.q: What does hertz count?
steps.why: Hertz is wiggles per second. The low a wiggles 220 times a second, so it is 220 hz.

whyWrong.1: Beats per minute is bpm, the speed of the beat. Hertz is the speed of the wiggle.
whyWrong.2: Bars are groups of four beats. Nothing to do with how fast the air moves.
whyWrong.3: A scale is a set of notes. Hertz measures one note's frequency.

steps.q: An octave up means the frequency
steps.why: Double the frequency, same note name, one octave up. 220 becomes 440.

whyWrong.1: It is not a fixed amount. 220 goes to 440, 440 goes to 880. Each octave doubles.
whyWrong.2: Halving the frequency takes you an octave down.
whyWrong.3: If nothing changed you would hear the same pitch.

steps.q: The low a was 220 hz. What is the a above it?
steps.why: Double 220 and you get 440. That is the a orchestras tune to.

whyWrong.1: 330 is one and a half times, which gives you a different note, not an a.
whyWrong.2: 240 is only a little higher, close enough to sound like an out of tune a.
whyWrong.3: 880 is two octaves up. Doubling twice.

steps.q: How many letter names do notes have before they repeat?
steps.why: Seven letters, a to g, then a again one octave higher.

whyWrong.1: Eight is the number of keys in this lesson, because the last one is a again.
whyWrong.2: There are twelve steps in an octave, counting the in between notes, but only seven letters.
whyWrong.3: Four is the beats in a bar. Notes use seven letters.

steps.q: Two notes an octave apart sound
options: like the same note, one higher
steps.why: Because one is exactly double the other, your ear hears them as the same note at two heights.

whyWrong.1: They share a name for a reason. The high a is the low a going twice as fast.
whyWrong.2: An octave is the most in tune two different notes can be.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is a separate thing. You can play an octave soft or hard.

steps.q: Which of these is a low frequency sound?
steps.why: The kick's body hums at around 50 hz, slow big pushes of air you feel in your chest.

whyWrong.1: Hi hats are mostly high frequencies, thousands of hertz, which is why they sound bright.
whyWrong.2: A whistle is a few thousand hertz, fast wiggles.
whyWrong.3: Birds sing high, usually well above 2,000 hz.

steps.q: Why do the keys in this lesson all sound good together?
options: they are from one scale that fits with a
they are all the same note
steps.why: The keys are picked from a scale built around a. Scales get their own lesson later.

whyWrong.1: They are different notes. Only the first and last share a name.
whyWrong.2: Only the first and last keys are an octave apart.
whyWrong.3: Volume has nothing to do with whether notes fit.

steps.next: Next: amplitude and volume. The same tune played soft, then hard, and why a song needs both.

lessons.title: amplitude and volume

song.why: how loud your melody sits against your beat decides whether it leads or hides

lessons.learn: What makes a sound loud, how loudness is measured, and setting how loud your melody sits in your song.
youCan: say what amplitude is and how it differs from pitch
say roughly what decibels measure
set your melody's level against your beat by ear

say.mentor:
Tap quiet, then loud. Same note, same pitch. The only difference is how hard the air is being pushed. Look at the picture: the wave is the same width, just taller.
That height is called amplitude. Bigger pushes of air reach your ear as a louder sound.
say.straight: Quiet vs loud. Same pitch, different amplitude: how far the air moves with each push. More amplitude, louder sound. The wave gets taller, not faster.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. Same note, but b is louder. A loud sound pushes the air harder, so the wiggle in the picture gets taller. It doesn't get faster, just bigger.

say.mentor:
Loudness is measured in decibels, written dB. The scale is odd but useful: every 6 dB or so roughly doubles the size of the wave, and about 10 dB sounds roughly twice as loud to most people.
In a music program you'll see a fader marked in dB, with 0 dB near the top. Pulling a part down by a few dB is how producers make room for something else without muting it.
say.straight: Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). About 6 dB doubles the wave's size, about 10 dB sounds twice as loud. Faders are marked in dB, with 0 near the top.
say.eli5: Grown-ups measure loudness with a number called decibels, or dB. Bigger number, louder sound. The sliders that make tracks louder or quieter are marked in dB.

deeper.title: how loud is loud
deeper.say: A quiet room is around 30 dB, a conversation around 60, a club near the speakers can pass 100. Long hours above about 85 dB can damage hearing, which is why DJs and producers wear earplugs at gigs and keep headphones at sensible levels.

deeper.title: velocity
deeper.say: On a keyboard or drum pad, how hard you hit is called velocity. It sets the amplitude of each note. Soft hits and hard hits in the same line are a big part of what makes playing sound human.

say.mentor:
Here's your song, with a level knob on your melody. Turn it down until the melody tucks in behind the beat, then up until it sits on top.
There's no right answer. A melody that's the star of the track sits loud. One that's more of a background colour sits lower. Leave it where your song sounds best to you.
say.straight: Your melody's level in your song. Down tucks it behind the beat, up puts it in front. Set it where it sounds right.
say.eli5: This knob makes your tune louder or quieter in your song. Turn it down and the boom takes over. Turn it up and your tune is the star. Stop where you like it.

say.mentor:
Songs don't stay at one level. A breakdown drops the drums so everything feels softer, then the drop hits harder because of it. Producers call this dynamics: the difference between the quiet and loud moments.
You'll build a breakdown and a drop in your song later. For now, notice it in the next track you hear: where does it get quieter, and how does it feel when it comes back?
say.straight: Dynamics is the contrast between quiet and loud moments. A drop feels big because the part before it was smaller. You'll build one later.
say.eli5: Songs get quiet sometimes and then loud again, and the loud bit feels extra exciting because of the quiet bit before it. That's called dynamics.

steps.q: Two notes have the same pitch but one is louder. What's different?
options: amplitude, how hard the air is pushed
steps.why: Loudness is amplitude. Pitch stays the same because the speed of the wiggle hasn't changed.

whyWrong.1: Frequency is pitch. Same pitch means same frequency.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the speed of the beat.

steps.q: What unit is loudness measured in?
steps.why: Decibels, dB. Hertz is for pitch, bpm for tempo.

whyWrong.1: Hertz measures frequency, the pitch.
whyWrong.3: Bars are for counting time.

steps.q: In the picture, what happened to the wave when the note got louder?
steps.why: More amplitude, a taller wave. The speed stays the same, so the pitch does too.

whyWrong.1: Faster would be a higher note.
whyWrong.2: Shape is tone colour, the next lesson.
whyWrong.3: It's the height that changes.

steps.q: Why does a drop feel bigger after a breakdown?
options: the quiet part before makes the loud part stand out
a drop is always 10 dB louder
steps.why: That contrast is dynamics. Loud only feels loud next to quiet.

whyWrong.1: The tempo usually stays the same.
whyWrong.2: There's no fixed number. It's the contrast you feel.
whyWrong.3: Key changes are a different trick.

steps.q: On a keyboard, what is velocity?
options: how hard you play each note
how long you hold a note
steps.why: Velocity is how hard you hit, and it sets each note's loudness.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.3: That's the note's length.

steps.next: Next: timbre. Why a saw sounds buzzy and a soft wave sounds round, and a filter to change your melody's colour.

lessons.title: timbre and tone colour

song.why: the same melody can sound soft and round or bright and buzzy, and the filter is how you choose

lessons.learn: Why a piano and a synth playing the same note sound different, what harmonics are, and a filter on your melody to change its colour.
youCan: say what timbre is
explain a bright sound as one with lots of harmonics
use a low pass filter to make your melody darker or brighter

say.mentor:
Tap through soft, saw and square. Same note, same loudness, three completely different characters. That character is called timbre, said "tam-ber", or tone colour. It's how you can tell a piano from a guitar even when they play the same note.
Look at the shapes. The smooth wave sounds round and pure. The sharp corners of the saw and the square are what make them bright and buzzy.
say.straight: Same pitch, same loudness, three timbres. Timbre (tone colour) is what makes instruments sound different on the same note. Sharp corners in the wave mean a brighter, buzzier sound.
say.eli5: Tap a, b and c. Same note each time, but they sound totally different: one is smooth like a flute, one is buzzy like a bee, one sounds like an old video game. That difference is called timbre.

say.mentor:
Here's the cool part. A buzzy sound isn't one pitch. It's the note you hear plus a stack of quieter, higher pitches riding on top of it, at two times, three times, four times the frequency and up. Those are called harmonics.
A pure, round wave has almost none. A saw has loads. Your ear blends them into one sound, and the mix of harmonics is the timbre. Sharp corners in the picture are what all those extra harmonics look like.
say.straight: A bright sound is the main note plus harmonics: quieter pitches at 2, 3, 4 times the frequency and up. A round wave has few, a saw has many. The mix of harmonics is the timbre.
say.eli5: Secret: a buzzy sound is really lots of sounds at once. There's the main note, plus a bunch of quiet higher notes hiding on top. They're called harmonics. Smooth sounds have hardly any. Buzzy ones have tons.

deeper.title: why octaves and fifths sound good
deeper.say: The first harmonics are twice and three times the note. Twice is the octave. Three times, brought down an octave, is the fifth. That's part of why those two intervals sound so at home together: they are already hiding inside a single note.

say.mentor:
Now change your own melody's colour. The cutoff knob is a filter: it lets the low part of the sound through and cuts the high harmonics. Turn it down and your melody gets darker and rounder, like hearing music through a wall. Turn it up and all the brightness comes back.
The shape knob picks the starting wave. Try a buzzy wave with the cutoff halfway: that's a classic synth sound.
say.straight: Cutoff is a low pass filter: down removes high harmonics (darker), up lets them back (brighter). Shape picks the starting wave. Set your melody's colour.
say.eli5: The cutoff knob is like a blanket over the speaker. Turn it down and the sound gets muffled and soft. Turn it up and it gets bright and clear again. The shape knob changes the wave. Play until you like how your tune sounds.

steps.q: A piano and a synth play the same note at the same volume. Why do they sound different?
options: different timbre, a different mix of harmonics
steps.why: Same note and loudness, different harmonics. That's timbre.

whyWrong.1: Same note means same pitch.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the speed of the beat, not one note.
whyWrong.3: Same volume means the same amplitude.

steps.q: What are harmonics?
options: quieter, higher pitches on top of the main note
steps.why: Pitches at two, three, four times the frequency and up, blended into one sound.

whyWrong.1: Chords are separate notes you play. Harmonics hide inside a single note.
whyWrong.2: An echo is a delayed copy. Harmonics happen at the same moment.
whyWrong.3: Beats are about rhythm.

steps.q: You turn the cutoff down on your melody. What happens?
options: it gets darker, the high harmonics are cut
steps.why: A low pass filter keeps the lows and cuts the highs, so the sound gets rounder and darker.

whyWrong.1: The note stays the same. Only its colour changes.
whyWrong.3: Turning it up brings brightness back.

steps.q: Which wave has the most harmonics?
steps.why: The saw's sharp drop is made of loads of harmonics, which is why it sounds the buzziest.

whyWrong.1: The round wave is nearly pure, with very few harmonics.
whyWrong.2: That's why they sound so different.
whyWrong.3: Everything except a pure sine has some.

steps.q: Why is it called a low pass filter?
options: it lets the low part pass and cuts the highs
it makes the sound low in volume
it passes the sound to a lower octave
steps.why: Lows pass through, highs above the cutoff are cut.

whyWrong.1: It changes colour, not overall volume.
whyWrong.3: The pitch stays the same.

steps.next: Next: waveforms. Sine, triangle, saw and square side by side, and the one that suits your melody.

lessons.title: waveforms

song.why: the wave you start from sets the whole character of your melody

lessons.learn: The four classic waves every synth starts from, what each is used for, and the one you pick for your melody.
youCan: name the sine, triangle, saw and square waves
say what each one is good for
pick a wave for your melody by ear

say.mentor:
Every synth sound starts life as a simple repeating shape. There are four classics, and you've heard three of them already. Tap through them again and really listen to the character.
The round one is close to a sine: pure, soft, almost no harmonics. The saw ramps up and drops: bright, buzzy, full of harmonics. The square jumps between two levels: hollow and reedy, the sound of old video games.
say.straight: The classic synth waves: sine (pure, soft), saw (bright, buzzy), square (hollow, reedy). The round one here is close to a sine.
say.eli5: Synths start from simple shapes. A smooth round one sounds soft and gentle. A pointy saw sounds buzzy. A blocky square sounds like an old video game. Tap them and listen.

say.mentor:
