lessons.title: notes and octaves

song.why: an octave jump in your melody is the same note made bigger, and it's one of the oldest tricks in a hook

lessons.learn: The twelve notes every melody is made from, why they repeat, and a melody in your song that jumps an octave.
youCan: say how many notes there are before the pattern repeats
say what an octave is
play the same note an octave apart in your melody

say.mentor:
Tap a, then b. Two different notes, but they sound like the same note, one lower and one higher. That gap is an octave, and the higher a is wiggling exactly twice as fast as the lower one.
This is the reason music has only twelve notes. Go up twelve steps from any note and you land on the same note again, an octave up.
say.straight: Same note, an octave apart. The higher one has double the frequency. Twelve steps up from any note brings you back to the same note an octave higher.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. They're the same note, one low and one high, like a dad and a kid singing the same song. That jump is called an octave.

say.mentor:
Western music uses twelve notes: c, c sharp, d, d sharp, e, f, f sharp, g, g sharp, a, a sharp, b. After b the pattern starts over at c, one octave higher. Each step to the very next note is called a semitone, so an octave is twelve semitones.
On a piano the black keys have two names. C sharp and d flat are the same key, named either way. There's no black key between e and f, or between b and c, because those pairs are already a semitone apart.
say.straight: Twelve notes, then they repeat an octave up. One step is a semitone; twelve make an octave. Black keys have two names (c sharp is d flat). E to f and b to c have no black key between.
say.eli5: There are only twelve notes. After the twelfth, they start again, higher. Black keys on a piano have two names, like a nickname.

deeper.title: octaves in numbers
deeper.say: The a above middle c is a4, 440 hz. One octave up, a5, is 880 hz. Every octave doubles the frequency, which is why the two notes blend so well.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Midi numbers every note, with 60 for middle c and 69 for a4. Live labels middle c as C3, while many other programs and most theory books call it C4. The midi number is the one that never changes.

say.mentor:
All twelve notes, including the black keys, are on this grid, one per row. Your lead is here. Find a note of your lead and tap the row twelve above it, in the same column: that's the same note an octave up. They sound like the same note, higher.
Now tap a square one row above or below one of your notes. That's a semitone, the smallest step on the keyboard, and the black keys live in those rows. Add one note an octave up and one a semitone away, play them, and keep whichever your lead likes.
say.straight: Rows are the twelve notes. Twelve rows up is the octave, the same note higher. One row is a semitone, where the black keys are. Add one of each.
say.eli5: Count twelve rows up: same note, higher. One row up: the tiniest step.

steps.q: How many notes before the pattern repeats?
steps.why: Twelve semitones, then the same notes again an octave up.

whyWrong.1: Seven is a scale, picked from the twelve.
whyWrong.2: Eight counts the first note twice, the octave.
whyWrong.3: Count every key, black and white, from c to the next c. Twelve.

steps.q: Going up one octave, the frequency
steps.why: A4 is 440 hz, a5 is 880 hz. Twice as fast.

whyWrong.1: Halving takes you an octave down.
whyWrong.2: It's a doubling, not a fixed step.
whyWrong.3: Then it would be the same note at the same height.

steps.q: C sharp and d flat are
options: the same key with two names
steps.why: One black key, named from the note below or the note above.

whyWrong.1: An octave is twelve semitones. These are the same note.
whyWrong.3: A fifth is seven semitones apart.

steps.q: Which note does Live call C3?
options: the lowest c on a piano
steps.why: Live names middle c C3. Many other programs call it C4.

whyWrong.1: That's an octave lower.
whyWrong.3: That's an a, not a c.

steps.next: Back to the melody path. Next: scales, and the scale your song will use.

lessons.title: the minor scale and its cousins

song.why: moving one note of the scale lifts a dark song without making it happy, and your melody follows

lessons.learn: How the natural minor scale is built, its cousins, and your own melody heard in natural minor and in dorian.
youCan: say the step pattern of natural minor
say what harmonic minor and dorian change
pick between minor and dorian for your song

say.mentor: Minor is a family, not one scale. They all share the darker sound you know, but each one moves a note or two, and each move changes the mood a little. Producers pick between them the way they'd pick between two shades of the same colour.
say.straight: Minor is a family of scales. Each one moves a note or two, and each move shifts the mood.
say.eli5: There isn't just one minor. There are a few cousins, all a bit moody, each one a little different.

say.mentor:
The plain one is natural minor. Its steps go whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. A whole step skips a key, a half step is the very next key.
Compared with major from the same home note, three notes are each a semitone lower: the third, the sixth and the seventh. That's where the darker sound comes from.
A minor and c major use exactly the same white keys. A minor just treats a as home. Every major key shares its notes with a minor key that starts on its sixth note, called its relative minor.
say.straight: Natural minor: whole, half, whole, whole, half, whole, whole. Against major on the same home note, the third, sixth and seventh are a semitone lower. A minor is the relative minor of c major.
say.eli5: Natural minor is a staircase with the small steps in different places from major. Three of its notes are a tiny bit lower, and that makes it sound moody.

say.mentor:
Here's your own song. Minor is natural minor. Dorian is its cousin: exactly the same, except the sixth note is a semitone higher.
Tap between them and listen to your melody. Wherever your tune uses that sixth note, it moves up a little and the darkness lifts, without turning happy. Dorian is all over funk, soul and jazz for that reason. If your melody never touches the sixth, you'll hear your chords and bass change instead. Keep the one that feels like your song.
say.straight: Your song in natural minor and in dorian. Dorian raises the sixth note by a semitone, so it's minor with a lift. Pick one.
say.eli5: Tap minor, then dorian. In dorian one note goes up a tiny bit, and your song sounds a little less gloomy. Pick the one you like.

say.mentor:
Two more cousins you'll meet. Harmonic minor raises the seventh note by a semitone instead. That seventh then sits right under home and pulls hard towards it, a dramatic, almost classical sound. Many dance tracks stay in natural minor and use the raised seventh only on one chord, right before they come home.
Melodic minor raises both the sixth and the seventh on the way up, and goes back to natural minor on the way down. It's common in jazz and rare in dance music.
say.straight: Harmonic minor raises the seventh, which pulls hard to home. Melodic minor raises the sixth and seventh going up, natural going down.
say.eli5: Two more cousins. One raises a note so it really wants to go home. The other changes depending on whether the tune goes up or down.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: In Live 12, give a midi clip a Root Note and a Scale Name and the piano roll marks the notes in that scale, so you can see a minor or dorian before you play a note.

steps.q: Compared with major from the same home note, natural minor lowers
steps.why: Those three notes, each a semitone lower, give minor its darker sound.

whyWrong.1: Home stays home.
whyWrong.2: The fifth stays the same in both.
whyWrong.3: Most notes are shared. Only three move.

steps.q: Dorian is natural minor with
steps.why: One note, the sixth, up a semitone. Minor with a lift.

whyWrong.1: Raising the third would make it sound major.
whyWrong.3: It still has seven notes.

steps.q: The relative minor of c major is
steps.why: Start on the sixth note of c major, a, and use the same white keys.

whyWrong.1: C minor has the same home as c major but different notes. That's its parallel minor.
whyWrong.2: E is the third note, not the sixth.
whyWrong.3: G is the fifth note, not the sixth.

steps.q: Harmonic minor raises which note?
steps.why: The raised seventh sits a semitone under home and pulls towards it.

whyWrong.1: Raising the third would turn it major.
whyWrong.3: Home never moves.

steps.next: Back to the melody path. Next: intervals, and a two-note phrase in your melody.

lessons.title: transposition and modes

song.why: a mode keeps your home note and changes the mood around it, so your song can go brighter or darker in one tap

lessons.learn: Moving a whole melody to a new key without changing its shape, what modes are, and your song heard in three modes on the same home note.
youCan: say what transposing does
say what a mode is
pick a mode for your song by ear

say.mentor:
Tap low, then high. Same sound, moved up. Now picture doing that to a whole melody: every note moves up by exactly the same amount. The tune keeps its shape perfectly, it just sits higher. That's transposing.
A song that's too high for a singer gets transposed down. A track that feels a bit flat can go up. The shape you wrote is safe either way.
say.straight: Transposing moves every note by the same amount. The distances between notes stay identical, so the melody keeps its shape, only higher or lower.
say.eli5: Tap a, then b. Same sound, higher. If you move every note of a tune up the same amount, it's the same tune, just higher. That's called transposing.

say.mentor:
Modes are a different trick. Take the white keys of c major, but treat d as home instead of c. Same seven notes, yet it sounds mysterious and a bit jazzy instead of bright. That's d dorian.
Each of the seven notes can be home, and each gives a mode with its own mood, because the pattern of big and small steps shifts around the new home. Ionian is the proper name for major, aeolian for natural minor. Dorian sits between them: darker than major, brighter than natural minor.
say.straight: A mode is the same set of notes with a different home. C major's notes with d as home is d dorian. Ionian is major, aeolian is natural minor, dorian sits between them.
say.eli5: Use the same notes but pick a different one to be home, and the whole song feels different. Each choice of home has a name, called a mode.

deeper.title: all seven modes
deeper.say: Ionian, major, bright. Dorian, minor with a brighter sixth, funk and soul. Phrygian, dark with a Spanish flavour. Lydian, dreamy and floating from its raised fourth, all over film scores. Mixolydian, major with a lowered seventh, blues rock. Aeolian, natural minor. Locrian, very tense and rarely used.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: In the piano roll, select notes and press the up or down arrow to move them a semitone, or hold Shift with the arrow to move them an octave. Audio clips have a Transpose control in the Clip View.

deeper.title: the key change lift
deeper.say: Moving a whole song up for its last chorus is called a modulation. Going up by a semitone or a tone right before the final chorus is a classic pop lift.

say.mentor:
Transposition moves the whole song up or down without changing a single interval, so it still sounds like your song, just higher or lower. Your song is playing. Turn shift and hear every melodic part move together while the drums stay put.
Up two semitones is a classic lift. Down five is a different mood entirely, darker and heavier. The key name updates as you turn. A singer might need it in a different key; a dj might want it to fit the next track. Keep the key where your song feels best.
say.straight: shift moves every melodic part together, in semitones. The drums stay. Keep the key that feels best.
say.eli5: Turn the knob and the whole song goes higher or lower, like singing the same tune in a higher voice.

steps.q: Transposing a melody up 5 semitones moves
steps.why: Every note moves the same amount, so the shape stays.

whyWrong.1: Moving one note changes the melody's shape.
whyWrong.2: Transposing is about pitch, not speed.
whyWrong.3: Transposing is about pitch, not volume.

steps.q: A mode is
options: the same notes with a different home
a faster version of a scale
steps.why: Pick a different note as home and the same notes take on a new mood.

whyWrong.1: Speed isn't part of it.
whyWrong.2: The modes of major all use seven notes.
whyWrong.3: Chords are built from a mode's notes, but a mode is a scale.

steps.q: D dorian uses the notes of which major scale?
steps.why: Dorian starts on the second note. D is the second note of c major, so it's the white keys.

whyWrong.1: D major has f sharp and c sharp. D dorian has neither.
whyWrong.2: G major has an f sharp. D dorian doesn't.
whyWrong.3: A major has three sharps.

steps.q: Which mode is major with a lowered seventh?
steps.why: Mixolydian, the sound of a lot of blues rock.

whyWrong.1: Lydian raises the fourth.
whyWrong.2: Dorian is minor with a raised sixth.
whyWrong.3: Phrygian is a dark minor sound.

steps.next: Melody done. Next path: harmony, starting with chords in your song.

lessons.title: chord types

song.why: swapping one chord for a different type changes the feeling of your whole song

lessons.learn: The four kinds of three-note chord, sevenths and sus chords, and minor, major and diminished chords played into your own song.
youCan: say how major, minor and diminished chords are built
say what a seventh and a sus chord add
hear the difference between chord types in your song

say.mentor: One note on its own has no mood yet. Stack two more on top of it and suddenly it's happy, sad, tense or dreamy, depending on exactly which two you pick. The kind of chord you build is called its type, or its quality.
say.straight: A chord's type, or quality, is decided by which notes are stacked on its root. Same root, different stack, different mood.
say.eli5: One note is just one note. Put two more on top and it can sound happy, sad or scary. Which notes you add decides the feeling.

say.mentor:
A triad is three notes. Count the semitones between them. Major stacks 4 then 3, and sounds bright. Minor stacks 3 then 4, and sounds dark. Diminished stacks 3 then 3, and sounds tense. Augmented stacks 4 then 4, and sounds floating and unfinished.
The only difference between major and minor is the middle note, one semitone apart. One tiny move, and the whole mood flips.
say.straight: Major 4 plus 3, bright. Minor 3 plus 4, dark. Diminished 3 plus 3, tense. Augmented 4 plus 4, floating. Major and minor differ by one semitone in the middle note.
say.eli5: Three-note chords come in four flavours: happy, sad, spooky and dreamy. Moving the middle note by one tiny step changes happy into sad.

say.mentor:
Now hear them in your song. This replaces your chords, so keep it at the end only if you like it.
Each pad is a chord built from your scale, and its label tells you the type. A small roman numeral is a minor chord. A capital one is major. The one with a little circle after it is diminished. Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play a minor one, then a major one, then the diminished one. Listen to how the diminished chord leans on the edge of its seat.
say.straight: Replaces your chords. Small numeral is minor, capital is major, the circle is diminished. Rec, count-in, then play one of each.
say.eli5: Press rec and wait for four ticks. Play a pad with a small letter (sad), a pad with a big letter (happy), and the pad with a tiny circle (spooky).

steps.hint: Lowercase numeral, then capital numeral, then the one with the circle.

say.mentor:
Add a fourth note a third above the top of a triad and you get a seventh chord. Major triad plus a major seventh is a major 7, lush and dreamy. Major triad plus a minor seventh is a dominant 7, bluesy and tense, itching to move. Minor triad plus a minor seventh is a minor 7, smooth and soulful.
A sus chord swaps the middle note for the second or the fourth. Without that middle note it's neither major nor minor, so it sounds open and undecided. Pop and electronic music use sus chords everywhere. The pads here play triads, so sevenths and sus chords are for when you write in Live.
say.straight: Sevenths add a fourth note. Major 7 is lush, dominant 7 tense, minor 7 smooth. Sus chords swap the middle note for the second or fourth, so they're open, neither major nor minor.
say.eli5: Add a fourth note and chords get fancier: dreamy, bluesy or smooth. Take out the middle note and the chord can't decide if it's happy or sad.

deeper.title: why diminished is tense
deeper.say: Three plus three semitones makes six from bottom to top, the tritone, the most unstable interval there is. That's also what's inside a dominant 7, and why both want to move on.

steps.q: A minor triad stacks
steps.why: Minor puts the smaller gap at the bottom.

whyWrong.1: That's major.
whyWrong.3: That's augmented.

steps.q: What makes a diminished chord tense?
steps.why: Three plus three is six semitones, the tritone, the most unstable interval.

whyWrong.1: A diminished triad has three notes.
whyWrong.2: Speed has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: Its bottom gap is a minor third, three semitones.

steps.q: A sus chord replaces the middle note with
steps.why: Suspended chords swap the third for a second or fourth, so they're neither major nor minor.

whyWrong.1: Adding the seventh makes a seventh chord.
whyWrong.2: An octave is the root again.
whyWrong.3: It still has three notes.

steps.q: Which seventh chord pulls hardest towards home?
steps.why: The tritone inside it wants to resolve.

whyWrong.1: Major 7 is lush and settled.
whyWrong.3: Sus 4 is open, but not a seventh chord.

lessons.title: keys and tonality

song.why: ending your progression on home sounds settled, ending away from it sounds like a question, and you choose which

lessons.learn: What a key is, why one note and one chord feel like home, and your progression ending at home or away from it.
youCan: say what a key and a tonic are
hear when a progression is home and when it isn't
end your progression where you want it

say.mentor:
Every song you know has a note it keeps coming back to. Hum the end of almost any tune and you'll land on it without thinking. That note is home, and the proper word for it is the tonic.
Your song has one too: the first key on your keys and the first pad on your chords. Everything else in the song pulls back towards it.
say.straight: Every song has a home note it returns to, called the tonic. In your song it's the first key and the first chord pad.
say.eli5: Songs have a home note, like a house they go back to at the end. Your song's home is the very first key.

steps.title: a key is a set and a home

say.mentor:
A key is seven notes plus the one that feels like home. In c major the notes are c d e f g a b, and c is home. In your song, the scale you picked gives the seven notes, and the first one is home.
Build a chord on each of those seven notes and you get the chords of the key. Roman numerals name them by position, so i is the home chord in a minor key and I in a major key. Notes and chords pull towards home with different strengths, and that pull is what makes a tune feel like it's going somewhere.
say.straight: A key is seven notes plus a home note, the tonic. A chord on each note gives the key's chords, named by roman numerals. Home is i in minor, I in major.
say.eli5: A key is a team of seven notes with one captain. The captain is home. Every chord in the song wants to get back to the captain's chord.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: In Live 12, give a midi clip a Root Note and a Scale Name and the piano roll marks the notes in the key. The Scale midi effect goes further and moves any note outside the scale to the nearest one inside it.

deeper.title: relative and parallel
deeper.say: C major and a minor share the same notes with a different home, called relative keys. C major and c minor share the same home with different notes, called parallel keys. Twelve major and twelve minor make 24 keys in all.

say.mentor:
Now feel it in your song. This replaces your chords, so you can keep it or not at the end.
Press rec, wait out the count-in, and play four chords, one per beat, ending on the first pad, home. Listen to it loop: it lands, settles, starts again. Then record it again, same first three chords, but end on any other pad. Hear that? It doesn't settle. It hangs there like a question, and the loop pulls you back to the start to answer it. Both are good. Keep the one your song wants.
say.straight: Replaces your chords. Record four chords ending on the first pad, home, and listen. Then record again ending elsewhere. Home settles, away sounds like a question. Keep one.
say.eli5: Press rec, wait for four ticks, and play four chord pads. Make the last one the first pad, home. Sounds finished, right? Try again and end on a different pad. Now it sounds like it isn't done yet.

steps.hint: The first pad is home. Play it last, then try ending on any other pad.

steps.q: The tonic is
options: the highest note in the song
steps.why: The tonic is home, the note and chord everything pulls back to.

whyWrong.1: Home can be any height.
whyWrong.2: Loudness has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: Speed is tempo.

steps.q: A key is
options: seven notes plus a home note
steps.why: A set of seven notes, with one of them as home.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.2: A key picks seven of the twelve.
whyWrong.3: You can start a song on any chord of the key.

steps.q: A progression that ends away from home sounds
steps.why: The pull towards home hasn't been answered yet.

whyWrong.1: That's ending on home.
whyWrong.3: All the chords are in the key. It's the ending that feels open.

steps.q: How many major and minor keys are there in all?
steps.why: Twelve major and twelve minor, one of each on every note.

whyWrong.1: That's only the major ones, or only the minor ones.
whyWrong.2: Seven is the number of notes in a key.
whyWrong.3: That's double the real count.
