options: plays the sound back again a moment later
adds the sound of a room
steps.why: Repeats, often in time with the beat.

whyWrong.1: That's reverb.
whyWrong.3: Effects don't change which notes play.

steps.q: Why does effect order matter?
options: each effect works on what came before it
only the last effect is heard
the first effect is always muted
steps.why: Reverb then distortion distorts the reverb too. Distortion then reverb keeps it clearer.

whyWrong.1: Swap two effects and you'll hear the difference.
whyWrong.2: Every effect in the chain is heard.
whyWrong.3: Nothing is muted.

steps.q: Which effect adds width with tiny shifts in pitch and timing?
steps.why: Chorus doubles the sound with small shifts, so it spreads wider.

whyWrong.1: Echo repeats the sound later.
whyWrong.3: An eq changes tone, not width.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try granulator iii to turn sound into a cloud.

lessons.title: granulator iii

song.why: chords that swell in and hang in the air like a cloud give your song a soft, floating layer

lessons.learn: How granular synthesis turns a recording into clouds of tiny grains, the controls that shape them, and a cloud-like swell on your own chords.
youCan: say what a grain is
say what position, grain size and spray do
turn your chords into a slow, floating swell

say.mentor:
Hats on the beats, then eighths, then sixteenths. The hits get closer and closer together. Keep going, hundreds of hits a second, each one a tiny overlapping sliver of sound, and you stop hearing hits at all. You hear a smooth, shimmering texture.
That's granular synthesis. It takes a recording and plays it as thousands of tiny overlapping pieces called grains. Even a single spoken word can become a long, glowing pad.
say.straight: Hits closer and closer together. Granular synthesis plays a recording as thousands of tiny overlapping pieces, grains, which blur into a smooth texture.
say.eli5: If you chop a sound into tiny, tiny bits and play lots of them at once, it turns into a soft, shimmery cloud. Those tiny bits are called grains.

say.mentor:
Position is where in the recording the grains come from. Move it and you scrub through the sound, so the colour morphs as you go. Put an lfo on it and the texture keeps slowly changing.
Grain size is how long each grain is. Big grains keep the recording recognisable and smooth. Tiny grains lose the original and get glitchy and buzzy.
Spray scatters where each grain starts, a little randomly, which makes the cloud shimmer instead of sounding frozen. Spread does the same thing across left and right, for width.
say.straight: Position: where in the recording grains come from. Grain size: big is smooth, small is glitchy. Spray: random start points for shimmer. Spread: random left and right for width.
say.eli5: Position picks which part of the sound to use. Grain size picks how big the bits are. Spray mixes them up a little so it sparkles.

deeper.title: granulator iii in live
deeper.say: Granulator III comes with Live 12. Drop a sample into it and play it from the keys: the keyboard sets the pitch of the grains. It's great on vocals, field recordings and any sound you want to hold suspended in time, and it can play grains backwards too.

say.mentor:
Our chords don't have a granular engine, so you'll make the kind of sound granular is loved for: a soft cloud that floats. Your song is playing.
Raise attack so each chord swells in instead of starting with a hit. Raise release so it hangs after the notes stop and the chords overlap. Spread widens the voicing, and send puts it in the reverb so it blurs at the edges. Keep it if your chords now float above the beat.
say.straight: Make your chords a cloud: longer attack to swell in, longer release to hang on, spread for width, send for reverb. Keep it.
say.eli5: Make your chords fade in slowly and fade out slowly. Add a big room with send. Now they float like a cloud.

steps.q: What is a grain?
options: a tiny piece of a recording
steps.why: Granular synthesis plays a recording as thousands of tiny overlapping pieces.

whyWrong.1: A loop is much longer than a grain.
whyWrong.2: A filter shapes tone; a grain is sound.
whyWrong.3: A note says what to play; a grain is the sound itself.

steps.q: You make the grains very small. What happens?
options: it gets glitchy and loses the original sound
steps.why: Tiny grains break up the recording's character into texture.

whyWrong.1: Bigger grains are smoother.
whyWrong.3: Size isn't level.

steps.q: What does spray do?
options: scatters where each grain starts, for shimmer
steps.why: Random start points keep the cloud moving and alive.

whyWrong.1: Level is separate.
whyWrong.3: Spray has nothing to do with reverb.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try collision, tension and electric for physical-model voices.

lessons.title: collision, tension, electric, analog

song.why: chords that strike and ring out like a struck or plucked instrument feel more played than a flat pad

lessons.learn: Physical modelling, synthesis that copies how real instruments make sound, Live's four modelled instruments, and a struck, ringing feel on your own chords.
youCan: say what physical modelling is
match Collision, Tension and Electric to the instruments they model
give your chords a struck or plucked feel

say.mentor:
A soft synth note that fades in and holds. Nothing about it says how it was made. Now think of a marimba: a mallet hits a wooden bar, the bar rings, the ring dies away. The sound comes from that physical event.
Physical modelling is synthesis that copies the event itself. Instead of oscillators and filters, it simulates a mallet hitting a bar, a string vibrating, a hammer striking a metal tine. Play harder and it doesn't just get louder, the tone changes, like the real thing.
say.straight: Physical modelling simulates how real instruments make sound: a mallet on a bar, a vibrating string, a hammer on a tine. Harder playing changes the tone, not just the level.
say.eli5: Some synths pretend to be real things: a stick hitting wood, a string being plucked. Hit harder and it sounds different, just like a real instrument.

say.mentor:
Collision models mallets striking things: marimbas, bells, kalimbas, metal. Tension models strings, plucked, hit or bowed. Electric models electric pianos, the hammers and tines of Rhodes and Wurlitzer-style keys.
Analog belongs to the same family in Live, though it's a little different: it models the circuits of a classic two-oscillator analog synth rather than an acoustic instrument.
say.straight: Collision: mallets, bells, marimbas. Tension: plucked and bowed strings. Electric: electric pianos. Analog: a modelled classic two-oscillator synth.
say.eli5: Collision is for things you hit, like bells. Tension is for strings. Electric is for electric pianos. Analog is an old-style synth.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Tension's controls describe a real string: its stiffness, its length, where the pickup sits, how hard the bow presses. Electric lets you shape the hammer, the tine and the pickup. Reach for these when a sampled instrument sounds static, because a model reacts to every note differently.

say.mentor:
Our chords aren't a physical model, but you can give them the shape of a struck instrument, and that shape is most of what your ear hears. Your song is playing.
Turn attack right down so every chord starts with a hit, like a mallet or a hammer. Set release so the chord rings and fades instead of stopping dead. Then lower cutoff a little: struck bars and electric pianos are warm, not fizzy. Keep it if your chords now feel played.
say.straight: Give your chords a struck shape: short attack, a release that rings, cutoff a bit lower for warmth. Keep it.
say.eli5: Make your chords start with a hit, ring out, and sound warm, like a bell or a piano.

steps.q: What does physical modelling simulate?
options: how a real instrument physically makes sound
steps.why: It models the mallet, string or hammer, not a recording of it.

whyWrong.1: Playing recordings is sampling.
whyWrong.3: Rooms are reverb.

steps.q: Which one models plucked and bowed strings?
steps.why: Tension simulates a vibrating string.

whyWrong.1: Collision is mallets and bars.
whyWrong.3: Analog is a classic synth.

steps.q: You play a physical model harder. What changes?
options: the tone, as well as the level
steps.why: Like a real instrument, a harder hit sounds different, not just louder.

whyWrong.1: That's what simpler instruments do.
whyWrong.2: Tempo isn't affected by how hard you play.
whyWrong.3: It reacts to every note.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try preset anatomy to take your lead apart.

lessons.title: preset anatomy

song.why: knowing what each knob on your lead does means you can fix it on purpose instead of by luck

lessons.learn: Every preset is built from the same few parts. Take your own lead apart one knob at a time and hear what each one was doing.
youCan: name the parts every preset is built from
tell a pad, a pluck, a bass and a lead apart by their envelopes
hear what each knob on your lead is doing

say.mentor:
Three shapes, the very first choice in any synth sound. A preset is a saved set of choices like this one, all made for you: a shape, a filter setting, an envelope, some movement, some effects.
Presets are a great way to learn, if you open them up. Change one knob, listen, put it back. Every choice in a good preset is there for a reason, and you can hear the reason.
say.straight: A preset is a saved set of choices: shape, filter, envelope, movement, effects. Change one knob at a time and listen to learn why it's set that way.
say.eli5: A preset is a sound someone already made and saved. Turn one knob at a time to see what each one does.

say.mentor:
Almost every synth preset is the same chain. An oscillator picks the raw shape. A filter sets the brightness. An amp envelope shapes the volume of each note over time, and a filter envelope moves the brightness. Modulation adds movement, and effects add space.
The amp envelope alone tells you a lot. A pad has a slow attack, holds, and fades out slowly. A pluck has a fast attack and dies away quickly. A bass starts instantly and stops cleanly.
say.straight: Oscillator, filter, amp envelope, filter envelope, modulation, effects. Slow attack and release is a pad, fast attack and quick decay is a pluck, fast and clean is a bass.
say.eli5: Every sound is built the same way: a shape, a brightness knob, and knobs for how each note starts and ends. A slow start sounds like a pad. A quick start and quick end sounds like a pluck.

deeper.title: opening a preset in live
deeper.say: Load any preset in Wavetable or Operator and read it in that order: oscillator shapes, filter cutoff and resonance, the amp envelope, the filter envelope, the modulation matrix, then the effects after the synth. Turn one control at a time and listen before you move on.

say.mentor:
Here are four of the knobs that make your lead what it is, with your song playing. Take it apart one at a time. Swing shape to each end and back: that's the raw wave. Sweep cutoff: that's the brightness. Turn env off and on: that's the brightness moving on each note. Shorten and lengthen release: that's how each note ends.
For each one, ask what your lead would lose without it. Then set them all where your song sounds best, and keep it.
say.straight: Four knobs on your lead: shape is the wave, cutoff is brightness, env is movement per note, release is how notes end. Move each one, hear what it does, set them and keep it.
say.eli5: Turn each knob all the way one way, then the other, and listen. Then put them where your tune sounds best.

steps.q: Slow attack, holding, slow release. What kind of preset is it?
steps.why: Fading in, holding and fading out is the pad shape.

whyWrong.1: A pluck starts fast and dies quickly.
whyWrong.3: A kick is a drum hit.

steps.q: What's the best way to learn from a preset?
options: change one knob at a time and listen
steps.why: One change at a time tells you exactly what each knob was doing.

whyWrong.1: Then you can't tell which change did what.
whyWrong.2: You learn by listening to changes.
whyWrong.3: The name doesn't tell you how it works.

steps.q: Which part of the chain mostly decides how bright a preset is?
steps.why: The filter cutoff lets more or fewer harmonics through.

whyWrong.1: The amp envelope shapes volume over time.
whyWrong.3: Pan is left and right.

steps.next: Back to your song path, or try build your own patch from scratch.

lessons.title: build your own patch

song.why: a lead voice you built yourself, step by step, is a sound nobody else's song has

lessons.learn: The order sound designers build a patch in, from a blank start to a finished voice, and your own lead built that way.
youCan: say the order a patch is built in
build a lead voice by ear, one stage at a time
use a reference track to judge your sound

say.mentor:
One plain synth note. This is close to what an init patch sounds like. Init means initialised: every knob at its starting point, no choices made yet. Sound designers often start here on purpose, so every part of the sound is a decision they made, not one they inherited.
Building from a blank start sounds slow, but there's an order to it, and once you know the order it goes fast.
say.straight: A plain note, close to an init patch, every knob at its start. Building from init means every choice is yours, and there's a set order to do it in.
say.eli5: This is a plain, empty sound. You're going to build your own sound from it, one step at a time.

say.mentor:
First the oscillator: pick the shape that has the right harmonics, soft for gentle, buzzy for bright. Then the filter: set how bright the sound is. Then the amp envelope: how each note starts and ends, which decides if it's a pad, a pluck or a lead. Then movement: a filter envelope or an lfo. Effects come last.
And keep checking by ear. Play a track you love next to yours and ask what's different. Brighter? Longer? Wider? Fix that one thing, then listen again.
say.straight: Oscillator, then filter, then amp envelope, then movement, then effects. Compare against a track you like and fix the biggest difference first.
say.eli5: First pick the shape. Then how bright. Then how notes start and stop. Then add wiggles and effects. Keep listening as you go.

deeper.title: init in live
deeper.say: In Wavetable, Operator or Drift, start from an init preset rather than a finished one, so nothing is decided for you. When your sound is done, save it as your own preset so you can use it again.

deeper.title: when it sounds wrong
deeper.say: Check the core first: the oscillator, the filter and the envelopes. Most problems with a patch live there, not in the effects.

say.mentor:
Build your lead, stage one: the tone. Your song is playing. Set shape first, soft, saw or square, for the harmonics you want. Add a little detune if you want it wide. Then set cutoff for how bright it should be, and res for how much bite sits at the edge of the filter.
Don't worry about getting it perfect. Get it close, then move on.
say.straight: Stage one, the tone. Set shape, add detune for width, set cutoff for brightness and res for bite.
say.eli5: Pick your sound's wave with shape. Make it wider with detune. Then make it brighter or darker with cutoff.

say.mentor:
Stage two: how it moves. Attack decides how each note starts, snappy or swelling. Release decides how it ends, clipped or trailing. Env makes the brightness move on every note. Echo goes last, to give your lead some space.
Now listen to the whole thing in your song. Something not right? Go back a stage. When it sounds like yours, keep it.
say.straight: Stage two, the movement. Attack and release for how notes start and end, env for brightness movement, echo for space. Keep it when it sounds like yours.
say.eli5: Now choose how each note starts and stops. Add env to make it shine and echo to make it repeat. Keep it when you love it.

steps.q: Which comes first when building a patch?
steps.why: The shape sets the harmonics everything else works on.

whyWrong.1: Effects come last.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect, so it's last too.
whyWrong.3: Tempo belongs to the song, not the patch.

steps.q: Your patch sounds wrong. Where do you look first?
steps.why: The core of the sound causes most problems.

whyWrong.1: Effects rarely cause the main problem.
whyWrong.3: Pan only moves it left or right.

steps.q: How does a reference track help?
options: it shows you what's different about your sound
steps.why: Comparing tells you the one thing to fix next.

whyWrong.1: You're comparing, not copying.
whyWrong.3: It's for listening, not processing.

steps.next: Back to your song path: levels and balance is next, where the mix starts.

lessons.title: the mixer in live

song.why: how loud your chords are and where they sit left to right is a mixer decision

lessons.learn: What a mixer is, the fader and pan on every part, and your chords placed on the stage by ear.
youCan: say what a fader, pan, solo and mute do
place your chords with level and pan
find the mixer in Live

say.mentor:
Every part of your song runs through a mixer on its way to your ears. Picture the desk at the back of a club: one channel strip per musician, each with a fader for how loud and a pan knob for where it sits, from left to right. All the strips add up into one master, and that's what comes out of the speakers.
Producers call that left to right picture the stage. Kick and bass stand in the middle, other parts step a little to the sides.
say.straight: A mixer has one strip per part. The fader sets how loud, pan sets left or right. Every strip adds up into the master.
say.eli5: A mixer is a big desk with a slider for every sound. Slide it up and that sound gets louder. Turn the pan knob and the sound moves left or right.

say.mentor:
Two buttons sit on every strip. Mute silences that part. Solo does the opposite: it plays that part alone and silences everything else, so you can hear exactly what one part is doing.
Solo is great for checking, but don't set levels with it. A part always sounds different on its own than it does inside the whole song.
say.straight: Mute silences one part. Solo plays one part alone. Check with solo, set levels with everything playing.
say.eli5: Mute makes one sound go quiet. Solo makes all the other sounds go quiet, so you only hear one.

deeper.title: the mixer in live
deeper.say: In Session view, each track's mixer sits at the bottom of its column: volume, pan, sends, mute, solo and a level meter. Every track ends up in the Master track, the sum of everything. Volume runs from minus infinity up to +6 dB, and pan from 50 left to 50 right.

deeper.title: cue
deeper.say: Cue lets you pre-listen to a track on headphones before anyone else hears it. For it to work, the Cue Out has to be set to a different output from the Master Out.

deeper.title: headroom
deeper.say: Pushing every fader up leaves no room at the top. Many engineers leave 3 to 6 dB of headroom on the master, turning tracks down rather than up.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with a channel strip on your chords. Bring the level down until the chords nearly vanish, then up until they fill the space behind your lead. Then pan them a little to one side and listen to the middle open up for your kick and bass.
There's no right spot. Leave them where your song feels balanced.
say.straight: Chords level: down until they nearly vanish, up until they fill the space. Pan a little off centre. Stop where it feels balanced.
say.eli5: Make your chords quieter, then louder, until they sound just right. Then turn pan to move them a little to one side.

steps.q: What does solo do?
steps.why: Solo silences everything else so you hear one part on its own.

whyWrong.1: That's mute.
whyWrong.2: Getting ready to record is the arm button.
whyWrong.3: Loudness is the fader.

steps.q: Why not set levels while a part is soloed?
options: a part sounds different alone than in the whole song
steps.why: Levels are about parts against each other, so set them with everything playing.

whyWrong.1: Solo doesn't change the part's volume.
whyWrong.3: Pan stays where it is.

steps.q: Where do all the strips end up?
steps.why: The master is the sum of every strip, the sound that leaves the speakers.

whyWrong.1: The first track is just one part.
whyWrong.2: Only what you send goes to the reverb.
whyWrong.3: Cue is a separate pre-listen output.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: mixing basics

song.why: levels, then tone, then space, in that order, is how a pile of parts turns into a mix

lessons.learn: The order most mixes follow, levels then eq then dynamics then space, worked through on your hats.
youCan: say the usual order of a mix
set a part's level before touching its tone
check a mix on more than one speaker

say.mentor:
Mixing means taking every part of your song and making them sit together as one record that sounds good anywhere: a phone, a car, a club. It sounds like a huge job, but most mixes follow the same order. Levels first, then eq, then dynamics, then space.
The order matters because each step builds on the one before. Eq fixes clashes between parts, but you can only hear a clash once the levels are roughly right.
say.straight: Mixing follows an order: levels, eq, dynamics, space. Each step builds on the last.
say.eli5: Mixing is making all your sounds fit together. You do it in steps: how loud first, then the tone, then the echoes.

say.mentor:
Levels: with faders only, get a rough balance. Most of a good mix is already here.
Eq: cut the clashes, like a lead fighting the bass down low. Dynamics: how much a part jumps between loud and quiet. A compressor evens that out. Space: reverb and echo give the mix depth, some parts close, some further back.
say.straight: Levels with faders. Eq to cut clashes. Dynamics, how much a part jumps between loud and quiet, with a compressor. Then reverb and echo for depth.
say.eli5: First make each sound the right loudness. Then fix sounds that bump into each other. Then add a little echo so some sounds feel far away.

deeper.title: reference tracks
deeper.say: Compare your mix with a released track you love. Match their loudness first: the louder of two mixes nearly always sounds better, even when it isn't.

deeper.title: more than one speaker
deeper.say: A good mix translates, meaning it sounds balanced on any system. Check on at least three: speakers, headphones and a phone. Mixes made only on headphones often come out wider than they should.

deeper.title: the mono check
deeper.say: Now and then, switch the master to mono. Anything that vanishes has a phase problem, and it will vanish on mono systems too.

deeper.title: breaks
deeper.say: Take a break every 45 to 60 minutes. Tired ears make bad decisions.

say.mentor: Mixing is placing every part. Start with your hats: level for how loud, high for how bright, send for how far away. Your song is playing.
say.straight: Hats first: level, high and send.
say.eli5: Make the hats the right loudness, brightness and distance.

say.mentor: Now your bass, the same way. Level against the kick, low for weight, and duck so it steps aside each time the kick hits. Both parts keep their settings when you add.
say.straight: Now the bass: level, low and duck under the kick.
say.eli5: Now the bass. Make it fit under the kick.

say.mentor: And your lead: level so it leads without shouting, pan it a little off centre, send for air. Three parts placed, and that's a mix.
say.straight: Now the lead: level, pan and send. Three parts placed.
say.eli5: Now the lead. Loudness, left or right, and space.

steps.q: What usually comes first in a mix?
steps.why: Get the balance roughly right with faders, then everything else is easier to hear.

whyWrong.1: Space comes last, once the parts sit together.
whyWrong.2: Dynamics come after levels and eq.
whyWrong.3: You can only judge tone once levels are set.

steps.q: In mixing, what does dynamics mean?
options: how much a part jumps between loud and quiet
where a part sits left or right
how much reverb a part has
steps.why: Dynamics is the range between loud and quiet. A compressor evens it out.

whyWrong.1: That's tempo.
whyWrong.3: That's space.

steps.q: Why match loudness before comparing your mix with a released track?
options: the louder one nearly always sounds better
it makes your mix louder for good
steps.why: Louder fools the ear. Match it and you hear the real differences.

whyWrong.1: You can compare anything once levels match.
whyWrong.3: Released tracks are usually loud.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: the signal chain

song.why: the order your lead's sound passes through things changes how it comes out

lessons.learn: What a signal chain is, why the order of effects matters, and your lead's chain from voice to reverb.
youCan: say what a signal chain is
say why the order of effects matters
shape your lead one stage at a time

say.mentor: A sound in a music program travels like water through pipes. It starts at the voice, the synth making the note, then flows through each effect in turn: a filter, some drive, a reverb. That path is called the signal chain, and every stage works on whatever the stage before it handed over.
say.straight: The signal chain is the path a sound takes: the voice, then each effect in order. Each stage changes what the last one made.
say.eli5: Your sound goes on a little trip through one machine, then the next. Each machine changes it a bit.

say.mentor:
Swap two stages and you get a different sound. An eq after a distortion shapes the gritty new sound the distortion made. Put it before, and the distortion roughs up whatever the eq left.
Reverb usually goes near the end. Put a compressor after a reverb and it squeezes the reverb tail too, so the whole thing pumps.
say.straight: Order changes the sound. Eq after distortion shapes the grit; before, it shapes what gets distorted. A compressor after a reverb makes the tail pump.
say.eli5: If you change which machine comes first, the sound comes out different. Echo usually goes last.

deeper.title: chains in live
deeper.say: Every track has a device chain. Sound flows through the devices from left to right, so the device on the left works first. Drag a device to a new spot and you change the order.

deeper.title: a common order
deeper.say: A common starting order is: an eq to cut problems, then dynamics like compression, then an eq to boost, then saturation, then modulation, then time effects like delay and reverb. It's a habit, not a rule.

deeper.title: bypass
deeper.say: Switch each device off and on to check it's earning its place. If you can't hear a difference, you may not need it.

say.mentor:
Here's your lead's chain, in order. Shape is the voice itself. Cutoff is the filter right after it. Drive roughs it up. Send passes a copy to the reverb at the end.
Move them one at a time, from the first to the last, and listen to each stage change what came before it. Keep the chain that makes your lead sound most like yours.
say.straight: Your lead's chain: shape (voice), cutoff (filter), drive, send (reverb). Set them in order, one at a time.
say.eli5: These four knobs are your lead's trip. Turn them one at a time, left to right, and hear each one change the sound.

steps.q: What is a signal chain?
options: the path a sound takes through each stage in order
a list of your song's parts
steps.why: Voice first, then each effect in turn, each working on what the last handed over.

whyWrong.1: Parts are tracks. The chain is inside one track.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is one stage in a chain.

steps.q: Why does the order of effects matter?
options: each stage works on what the last one handed it
effects only work first in line
the last effect is always loudest
steps.why: Change the order and each stage gets a different sound to work on.

whyWrong.1: Every stage in the chain works.
whyWrong.3: It matters on any part.

steps.q: In Live, which way does sound flow through a track's devices?
steps.why: The device on the left works first.

whyWrong.1: It's the other way round.
whyWrong.2: The device chain runs across, not up.
whyWrong.3: Each device works in turn.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: groups and routing

song.why: shaping your whole drum kit at once makes the drums sound like one instrument

lessons.learn: What a group is, where a part's sound goes next, and your drum kit shaped as one.
youCan: say what a group and a bus are
shape several parts at once
group tracks in Live

say.mentor:
Your kick and clap are separate sounds, but they live together in your drum kit and come out through one channel. That's a group: several parts added together into one strip, so one fader or one eq moves them all at once.
Producers group drums, synths and vocals, so a mix with forty parts can be handled as five or six.
say.straight: A group adds several parts into one strip. One fader or eq then moves them all together.
say.eli5: A group is like a box with lots of sounds inside. Turn the box's knob and every sound inside changes together.

say.mentor:
Routing is where each part's sound goes next. By default every part flows straight to the master. Point a few parts into a group instead and the group becomes a little mix of its own, called a bus: one channel carrying several parts, before everything reaches the master.
That's why you can compress your whole kit together, so every hit squeezes as one.
say.straight: Routing decides where a sound goes next. Send parts to a group and it becomes a bus, a channel carrying several parts mixed together.
say.eli5: Every sound goes somewhere next, like a road. You can send lots of sounds down the same road, then change them all at once.

deeper.title: groups in live
deeper.say: Select tracks and press Cmd+G on a Mac or Ctrl+G on Windows to group them. The group track is a real audio bus with its own devices, mixer strip, sends and automation. Groups can sit inside other groups.

deeper.title: audio to and audio from
deeper.say: Each track has Audio To and Audio From menus. A track's output can go to the master, a group or another track's input. Resampling, in Audio From, records Live's master output onto an audio track.

deeper.title: glue on the group
deeper.say: A common move is a Glue Compressor on the drum group, so every drum is compressed together.

say.mentor: A group is several tracks through one channel. Your kick and clap share this channel: turn low, mid, high and drive and both move. Your song is playing.
say.straight: Kick and clap through one channel.
say.eli5: The drums all go through one channel.

say.mentor: Your hats are the other member of the drum group. Match the drive you gave the kick and clap so the group sounds like one kit, then set their level in it. In Live you'd make one group track and put all three inside.
say.straight: Hats join the group: match the drive, set the level.
say.eli5: Hats join the drums. Make them sound like one kit.

steps.q: What is a group?
options: several parts added together into one strip
steps.why: One strip for several parts, so they can be shaped together.

whyWrong.1: Groups hold parts inside one song.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect. A group can hold effects.
whyWrong.3: The parts inside stay different.

steps.q: What is a bus?
options: a channel carrying several parts mixed together
steps.why: A group is a bus. So is the master.

whyWrong.1: A bus carries sound, it doesn't make it.
whyWrong.2: Tempo is the speed of the song.
whyWrong.3: Patterns are notes. A bus is where sound flows.

steps.q: Why group your drums?
options: to shape them all at once, like one instrument
steps.why: One move on the group changes every drum inside it.

whyWrong.1: Grouping doesn't touch timing.
whyWrong.2: Every part in the group stays.
whyWrong.3: Grouping doesn't change stereo.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, eq, a place for everything.

lessons.title: eq eight

song.why: three bands of eq decide how deep, how solid and how clear your bass sounds

lessons.learn: Lows, mids and highs, what lives where, and three bands of eq on your bass.
youCan: say roughly where lows, mids and highs sit
clean up a muddy sound with a small cut
shape your bass with three bands

say.mentor:
An eq splits a sound into ranges of frequency and lets you turn each one up or down. Roughly: the lows, from about 20 to 200 hz, are weight and boom. The mids, from about 200 hz to 3 khz, are the body of a sound. The highs, above about 3 khz, are bite, clarity and air.
Your bass lives mostly in the lows, but its mids and highs are what let you hear it on small speakers.
say.straight: Lows, about 20 to 200 hz: weight. Mids, 200 hz to 3 khz: body. Highs, above 3 khz: bite and air.
say.eli5: Every sound has a deep part, a middle part and a high part. An eq lets you turn each part up or down.

say.mentor:
A lot of muddy mixes have too much going on between about 200 and 500 hz, where many parts overlap. A small cut there often cleans a sound up more than any boost would.
Cutting first is a good habit: take away what's in the way before you add anything.
say.straight: Mud usually lives around 200 to 500 hz. A small cut there cleans things up. Cut before you boost.
say.eli5: When sounds get muddy, take a little bit away from the middle. Taking away often works better than adding.

deeper.title: eq eight in live
deeper.say: EQ Eight has eight bands. Each band has a shape: low cut and high cut remove everything past a frequency, shelves tilt a wide region up or down, a bell boosts or cuts around one point, and a notch removes one narrow frequency.

deeper.title: frequency, gain and q
deeper.say: Each band has three controls. Frequency is where it works, gain is how much it boosts or cuts, and Q is how wide or narrow the band is. A narrow Q is surgical, for hunting one ringing note. A wide Q is musical, for shaping tone.

deeper.title: mid and side
deeper.say: In M/S mode, EQ Eight works on the middle of the stereo picture and on the sides separately. Cutting the lows on the sides keeps the low end mono and tight.

say.mentor:
Your bass with three bands. Low is the weight: a little up for more boom, down if it's swamping your kick. Mid is the body, and where a bass turns muddy, so try a small cut. High is the edge that lets a bass come through on a phone speaker.
Keep the moves small and keep listening to the whole song.
say.straight: Low: weight, down if it swamps the kick. Mid: try a small cut for less mud. High: edge for small speakers.
say.eli5: Turn low for more or less boom. Turn mid down a little if it sounds muddy. Turn high for a bit of edge.

steps.q: Roughly where do the lows sit?
steps.why: About 20 to 200 hz is weight and boom.

whyWrong.1: That's the highs.
whyWrong.3: Each range has its own place.

steps.q: A sound is muddy. Where might you try a small cut?
steps.why: That's where lots of parts overlap and build up.

whyWrong.1: That's air, not mud.
whyWrong.2: That's below what most of us hear.
whyWrong.3: Boosting usually adds more mud.

steps.q: In EQ Eight, what does Q set?
options: how wide or narrow a band is
steps.why: Narrow for surgery, wide for tone.

whyWrong.1: That's the frequency control.
whyWrong.3: There are always eight.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, space, reverb and echo.

lessons.title: effects overview

song.why: one effect from each family on your lead shows you what each family is for

lessons.learn: The main families of effects, the problem each one solves, and one of each on your lead.
youCan: name the main families of effects
pick a family for a problem
try eq, drive, echo and reverb on your lead

say.mentor:
There are thousands of effects, but almost all of them belong to a handful of families. Learn the families and you can reach for the right tool fast, instead of guessing.
This plain synth note is a blank page. Every family would change it in its own way.
say.straight: Thousands of effects, a handful of families. Know the families and you know which tool to reach for.
say.eli5: There are lots of effects, but they come in a few families, like a family of cats and a family of dogs.

say.mentor:
Eq shapes tone by frequency. Dynamics, like compressors and limiters, control loud and quiet. Time effects, reverb and echo, put a sound in a space. Saturation, or drive, adds grit and warmth by roughing up the wave. Modulation, like chorus and phaser, makes a sound move by wobbling it with a slow wave called an lfo. Utility tools do plain jobs like gain and stereo width.
Each family fixes a different problem. Too dull is an eq job. Jumping between loud and quiet is a dynamics job.
say.straight: Eq: tone. Dynamics: loud and quiet. Time: reverb and echo. Saturation: grit. Modulation: movement. Utility: gain and width. Match the family to the problem.
say.eli5: Eq changes the tone. Dynamics change loud and quiet. Reverb and echo add space. Drive adds crunch. Pick the one that fixes your problem.

deeper.title: the families in live
deeper.say: Live's own devices cover every family: EQ Eight for eq, Compressor, Glue Compressor and Limiter for dynamics, Reverb, Hybrid Reverb and Delay for time, Saturator for drive, and Utility for gain and width.

deeper.title: fewer is better
deeper.say: Learn one effect in each family well before collecting more. The effects that come with your music program are often plenty. Switch each one off and on, and if you can't hear it helping, take it out.

deeper.title: insert or send
deeper.say: Reverb and delay usually go on a send that many parts share. It uses less processing power and puts everything in the same space.

say.mentor:
One effect from each family on your lead. High is eq: a little brighter or darker. Drive is saturation: grit. Echo and send are time: repeats, and a room.
Try each one on its own first, then together. Keep only the ones that make your lead better, and set the rest back to where they were.
say.straight: High is eq, drive is saturation, echo and send are time effects. Try each alone, then together. Keep what helps.
say.eli5: Try each knob on your tune, one at a time. Keep the ones that make it sound better.

steps.q: Which family is reverb in?
steps.why: Reverb and echo put a sound in a space.

whyWrong.1: Eq shapes tone by frequency.
whyWrong.3: Saturation adds grit.

steps.q: A part jumps between loud and quiet too much. Which family helps?
steps.why: A compressor evens out loud and quiet.

whyWrong.1: Reverb and echo add space, not control.
whyWrong.3: Eq is about tone, not loudness over time.

steps.q: What does drive do?
options: adds grit and warmth by roughing up the wave
puts the sound in a room
steps.why: Drive is saturation, the grit family.

whyWrong.1: That's reverb.
whyWrong.3: That's echo.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, space, reverb and echo.

lessons.title: sends and returns

song.why: sending your chords into a shared reverb puts them in the same room as your other parts

lessons.learn: What a send and a return are, why one shared reverb glues a mix, and how much of your chords to send.
youCan: say what a send and a return are
set how much of a part goes to the reverb
make a return track in Live

say.mentor: Picture a band playing in one hall. Everyone shares the same room, and that shared space is a big part of why they sound like one band. Mixes copy this with one reverb that every part can feed into, a little or a lot.
say.straight: One shared reverb puts every part in the same room, which helps them sound like one record.
say.eli5: If all your sounds play in the same big room, they sound like they belong together.

say.mentor:
A return is a channel that holds an effect, usually a reverb or a delay, and nothing else. A send is a knob on each part that decides how much of that part gets copied over to the return. The dry part keeps playing as it was, and the return adds the room underneath.
So with one reverb you can give the lead a lot, the chords some and the kick none. By default a send comes after the fader, so turning a part down turns its reverb down too.
say.straight: A return holds a shared effect. Each part's send sets how much goes to it. The dry part stays. Sends follow the fader by default.
say.eli5: There's one echo room. Each sound has a knob that says how much of it goes into the room.

deeper.title: returns in live
deeper.say: Cmd+Alt+T on a Mac or Ctrl+Alt+T on Windows makes a return track. Put a Reverb on it, and every track gets a send knob for it.

deeper.title: pre and post
deeper.say: Sends are post-fader by default, so the send follows the track's fader. Switch one to pre-fader and it ignores the fader, handy when you want the reverb to keep going while the dry track is turned down.

deeper.title: why share
deeper.say: One reverb on a return uses far less processing power than a reverb on every track, and it puts every part in the same room. Returns can even send to other returns.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Send feeds your chords into the reverb, the same way a send feeds a return in Live. Turn it up and the chords move back into the room, behind your lead. Turn it down and they come close and dry.
Chords and pads often get more reverb than drums. Find the amount where they sit behind your lead without going blurry.
say.straight: Send sets how much of your chords goes to the reverb. Up moves them back, down brings them close. Stop before they blur.
say.eli5: Turn send up and your chords sound further away, in a big room. Stop before they get blurry.

steps.q: What does a send do?
options: copies some of a part to a return
steps.why: The dry part stays. A copy goes to the shared effect.

whyWrong.1: The dry sound keeps playing.
whyWrong.3: The part still plays.

steps.q: Why share one reverb across parts?
options: it puts every part in one room and uses less power
you can only have one effect
steps.why: One room glues the mix, and one reverb is lighter than many.

whyWrong.1: Tempo doesn't change.
whyWrong.2: You can have lots of effects.
whyWrong.3: It's about space, not level.

steps.q: By default, you turn a part's fader down. What happens to its reverb?
steps.why: Sends come after the fader by default, so they follow it.

whyWrong.1: Less part, less reverb.
whyWrong.3: It follows the fader down, it doesn't stop.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, glue, compression and loudness.

lessons.title: reverb and delay

song.why: a little room or a little echo on your drums changes how far away they feel

lessons.learn: Reverb and delay up close, predelay and feedback, and both tried on your drums so you can keep one.
youCan: say how reverb and delay differ
say what predelay and feedback do
choose reverb or echo for your drums

say.mentor:
Reverb and delay both add space, in very different ways. Reverb is the sound of a room: thousands of reflections smearing into a tail. Delay is a clear copy of the sound coming back, once or many times.
Here's a kick and clap with neither. Imagine the clap ringing out in a hall, or bouncing back off a far wall as an echo.
say.straight: Reverb: a room, reflections smeared into a tail. Delay: clear repeats. This is the dry version.
say.eli5: Reverb sounds like clapping in a big hall. Delay sounds like shouting in a canyon and hearing it come back.

say.mentor:
Predelay is a short gap before a reverb starts. With a little predelay, around 30 ms, the hit comes through clean before the room arrives, so the sound stays clear.
Feedback is how much of each echo is fed back into the delay to echo again. Low feedback gives one or two repeats. Push it near the top and the repeats pile up and can run away.
say.straight: Predelay: a short gap before the reverb, so the hit stays clear. Feedback: how many times a delay repeats. Too much runs away.
say.eli5: Predelay makes the room wait a tiny moment before it starts. Feedback is how many echoes you get.

deeper.title: reverb in live
deeper.say: Live's Reverb builds its tail from an input filter, predelay, early reflections and a longer decay. Hybrid Reverb adds convolution, which uses a recording of a real space.

deeper.title: delay in live
deeper.say: The Delay device has a line for each side. Each can sync to the grid or run free in milliseconds, with its own feedback and a filter on the repeats, so each echo gets duller or thinner. Ping Pong bounces the echoes from left to right, and Freeze holds the current echoes while the sound moves on.

deeper.title: on a return
deeper.say: Both usually live on return tracks, so many parts share one space. A common move is a high-pass on the reverb return around 200 hz, so the room doesn't muddy the low end.

say.mentor: Reverb and delay on your drums. send is reverb, a room; echo is delay, repeats. Your song is playing. Keep the kick's send low so the low end stays tight.
say.straight: Reverb (send) and delay (echo) on the drums. Keep send low for the kick.
say.eli5: Room and repeats on the drums.

say.mentor: Now your hats, which can take much more. Send them further back and give them a touch of echo. Two parts, two different amounts, which is the point: space is per part.
say.straight: Now the hats, with more of both. Space is set per part.
say.eli5: Hats can go further away. Try it.

steps.q: What's the difference between reverb and delay?
options: reverb is a smeared room, delay is clear repeats
steps.why: Reverb smears, delay repeats.

whyWrong.1: Loudness isn't the difference.
whyWrong.3: They sound very different.

steps.q: What does predelay do?
options: leaves a short gap so the hit stays clear
steps.why: The dry hit comes first, then the room.

whyWrong.1: That's the decay.
whyWrong.3: The reverb still plays, just a moment later.

steps.q: What happens if you push delay feedback near the top?
options: the repeats pile up and can run away
steps.why: Each echo feeds the next, so they keep building.

whyWrong.1: It does the opposite.
whyWrong.3: Tempo isn't touched.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, glue, compression and loudness.

lessons.title: hybrid reverb

song.why: a bigger, longer space behind your chords makes your song feel wide and deep

lessons.learn: Two ways to make a reverb, recorded rooms and built ones, and a bigger space behind your chords.
youCan: say what convolution and algorithmic reverb are
give your chords a bigger space
say why big reverbs belong on a return

say.mentor: Not every reverb is made the same way. Some play back a recording of a real space. Others build the tail with maths. Live's Hybrid Reverb runs both at once and lets you blend them, which is how you get a space that sounds real and huge at the same time.
say.straight: Some reverbs use recordings of real spaces, some are built with maths. Hybrid Reverb blends both.
say.eli5: One kind of reverb copies a real room. Another kind is made up by the computer. Hybrid Reverb mixes them together.

say.mentor:
Convolution reverb uses an impulse response: a recording of how a real hall, room or plate rings out after a sharp sound. Run your chords through it and they take on the sound of that place.
Algorithmic reverb builds the tail with maths instead. It can't copy a real room exactly, but it can make tails no real room could, long and moving.
say.straight: Convolution: a recording of a real space, applied to your sound. Algorithmic: a tail built by maths, able to do things real rooms can't.
say.eli5: Convolution is like a photo of a real room's echo. Algorithmic is like a painting of an echo that could never be real.

deeper.title: hybrid reverb in live
deeper.say: Hybrid Reverb has a convolution engine and an algorithmic engine side by side, with a blend between them, plus predelay and eq. Freeze holds the current tail for as long as you like.

deeper.title: share it
deeper.say: Long convolution reverbs use a lot of processing power. Put one on a return and share it, rather than loading one on every track.

deeper.title: keep some predelay
deeper.say: Skip predelay and a big reverb can swallow the sound going into it. A short gap keeps the source clear.

say.mentor:
Here's your song. Turn send up for more room behind your chords. Then try release, how long each note keeps sounding after it ends: longer notes ring into the reverb and the space feels bigger.
Too much of both and the chords wash over everything. Back off until your lead still sits clearly on top.
say.straight: Send for more room. Release, how long notes ring after they end, makes the space feel bigger. Stop before the chords wash out the lead.
say.eli5: Turn send up for a bigger room. Turn release up so the notes ring longer. Stop before it gets too blurry.

steps.q: What does a convolution reverb use?
options: a recording of a real space
steps.why: An impulse response, how a real place rings.

whyWrong.1: That's algorithmic reverb.
whyWrong.3: Reverb doesn't follow tempo.

steps.q: What can algorithmic reverb do that a recorded room can't?
options: make tails no real room could
sound exactly like one real hall
steps.why: It's built with maths, so it isn't limited to real spaces.

whyWrong.1: That's what convolution is best at.
whyWrong.3: Reverb doesn't change tempo.

steps.q: Why share one big reverb on a return?
options: long reverbs use a lot of processing power
steps.why: One shared reverb is far lighter than many.

whyWrong.1: Level is up to the sends.
whyWrong.2: You can put reverb on a track too.
whyWrong.3: Swing is timing.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, glue, compression and loudness.

lessons.title: glue compressor

song.why: a gentle squeeze on the whole song makes your parts move together like one record

lessons.learn: What a bus compressor does, how much is enough, and glue on your whole song.
youCan: say what a compressor does
say how much glue is usually enough
hear when glue starts to pump

say.mentor:
A compressor turns a sound down when it gets loud, then lets it back up. Put a gentle one across your whole song and every part starts to breathe together. Engineers call that glue.
When it's working you barely notice it. When it's missing, the parts sound like separate sounds that happen to be playing at the same time.
say.straight: A compressor turns loud moments down. A gentle one on the whole song makes the parts move together: glue.
say.eli5: A compressor is like a hand that turns the sound down a little when it gets too loud. It makes all your sounds feel stuck together.

say.mentor:
Glue is subtle. Gain reduction is how much the compressor is turning things down at any moment, and on a master engineers usually aim for about 1 to 3 dB of it.
Push it to 6 dB or more and you start to hear it pump: the whole mix ducking on every kick. Sometimes that's the sound you want. On a master, usually not.
say.straight: Gain reduction is how much it turns down. For glue, about 1 to 3 dB. At 6 dB or more it pumps.
say.eli5: A little bit of squeeze is glue. Too much and the whole song bounces up and down with the kick.

deeper.title: glue compressor in live
deeper.say: Live's Glue Compressor is modelled on a classic console bus compressor. A common bus setting is a ratio of 4 to 1, attack around 10 ms and release on auto, then threshold down until the meter shows 1 to 3 dB of gain reduction.

deeper.title: the sidechain filter
deeper.say: Its sidechain high-pass filter stops the kick's lowest notes from driving the compressor, so the whole mix doesn't duck on every beat.

deeper.title: a little in two places
deeper.say: Many producers use a light Glue Compressor on the drum group and another on the master, rather than a lot in one place.

deeper.title: check with bypass
deeper.say: Switch it off and on. If you can't hear any difference, it may not be doing much.

say.mentor:
Your whole song, with glue on the master. Turn glue up slowly and listen to your drums and bass lock together. Keep going until you hear the mix pump on the kick, then back off to just before that. That's usually the sweet spot.
Leave out where it is for now. The next lesson is all about it.
say.straight: Turn glue up until you hear pumping, then back off a little. Leave out alone for now.
say.eli5: Turn glue up until your song starts to bounce, then turn it back down a little.

steps.q: What does a compressor do?
options: turns a sound down when it gets loud
steps.why: Loud moments come down, then it lets go.

whyWrong.1: That's a delay.
whyWrong.3: Tempo stays the same.

steps.q: How much gain reduction do engineers usually aim for as glue on a master?
steps.why: Glue is subtle. More starts to pump.

whyWrong.1: That would squash the life out of it.
whyWrong.3: Too much pumps and tires the ear.

steps.q: What does too much glue sound like?
options: the whole mix pumps on every kick
steps.why: The compressor ducks everything each time the kick hits.

whyWrong.1: Tempo doesn't change.
whyWrong.2: The hats get squeezed too, but they don't vanish.
whyWrong.3: A compressor adds no space.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, sections. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: limiter and true peak

song.why: a limiter lets your song get loud without ever clipping

lessons.learn: What a limiter does, gain and ceiling, true peaks, and how loud your song can go before it loses punch.
youCan: say what a limiter and clipping are
say what a true peak is
push your song loud without losing the kick

say.mentor:
A limiter is the last thing on almost every master. It's a hard ceiling: nothing gets past it. You push your song up into it, and it flattens any peak that would go over, so the song gets louder without clipping.
Clipping is what happens when a sound goes past the top of what can be played. The top of the wave gets cut off flat, and you hear crackle and crunch.
say.straight: A limiter is a ceiling nothing can pass. Push the song into it to get louder without clipping, the crunch of a wave cut off flat.
say.eli5: A limiter is like a low ceiling. The song can get loud, but it can never bump its head and crackle.

say.mentor:
A limiter has two main controls. Gain pushes your song up into it. Ceiling sets the highest level anything can reach.
There's a sneaky problem. A digital file stores the wave as dots, called samples. Between the dots, the real wave can swing a little higher than any of them, and those in-between peaks, called true peaks, can still clip when the file plays. Streaming formats like mp3 add a few more. That's why many engineers set the ceiling to -1 dB true peak for streaming.
say.straight: Gain pushes in, ceiling is the limit. True peaks hide between samples and can still clip, so streaming masters often use a -1 dB true peak ceiling.
say.eli5: Sometimes the wave sneaks a tiny bit higher between the dots the computer saves. So you leave a small gap under the ceiling, just in case.

deeper.title: limiter in live
deeper.say: Live's Limiter has Gain, Ceiling and a lookahead setting, which lets it see a peak coming a few milliseconds early and turn down smoothly. Its True Peak option catches the peaks between samples.

deeper.title: two stages
deeper.say: A common chain is a Glue Compressor on the master, then the Limiter last, so the loudness work is split and neither has to work too hard.

deeper.title: fix the mix first
deeper.say: A limiter is polish. If a mix sounds wrong, fix the parts. Pushing a limiter harder won't.

deeper.title: louder fools you
deeper.say: When you compare with the limiter on and off, match the loudness. Louder almost always sounds better at first, even when it's squashing the punch out.

say.mentor:
Your whole song. Out sets how hard your song hits the limiter. Turn it up and the song gets louder while the limiter stops it clipping.
Push further and listen to the kick: it starts to lose its punch, flattened against the ceiling. Find the loudest point where the kick still hits.
say.straight: Out sets how hard the song hits the limiter. Turn up until the kick starts losing punch, then back off.
say.eli5: Turn out up to make your song louder. If the boom starts to sound flat, turn it back down a little.

steps.q: What does a limiter do?
options: stops anything going past a set ceiling
steps.why: It's a hard ceiling. Nothing gets over it.

whyWrong.1: Reverb is a time effect.
whyWrong.3: It's usually used to make songs louder.

steps.q: What is clipping?
options: a sound going past the top, cut off flat and crunchy
steps.why: The top of the wave gets chopped off, and you hear it.

whyWrong.1: A sample is different.
whyWrong.3: Eq is tone.

steps.q: Why set a ceiling around -1 dB true peak for streaming?
options: it leaves room for peaks between samples and from streaming formats
true peak means the quietest point
steps.why: Those hidden peaks can still clip, so you leave a little space.

whyWrong.1: Loud songs are allowed.
whyWrong.3: It's the highest point, between samples.

steps.q: Pushing a limiter too hard does what?
options: squashes the punch out of the kick
steps.why: The kick's peaks get flattened against the ceiling.

whyWrong.1: It gets louder, not quieter.
whyWrong.2: The bass stays, it just gets squashed too.
whyWrong.3: A limiter adds no echo.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, sections. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: racks and macros

song.why: moving the filter and the space together turns two settings on your lead into one sweep

lessons.learn: What a rack and a macro are, how a macro's ranges work, and two of your lead's knobs moved as one.
youCan: say what a rack and a macro are
say how one macro can move knobs in opposite directions
map a parameter to a macro in Live

say.mentor: Build a sound with a filter, an echo and a reverb and you've got a dozen knobs. A rack wraps all those devices into one, and a macro is a big knob on the front that turns several of the knobs inside at once. One twist, and the filter opens while the reverb rises.
say.straight: A rack wraps several devices into one. A macro is one knob that turns several knobs inside it.
say.eli5: A macro is one big knob that turns lots of little knobs at the same time.

say.mentor:
Each knob a macro moves gets its own range, a minimum and a maximum. So one macro can sweep your cutoff all the way while only nudging the reverb a little.
Flip a range, maximum below minimum, and that knob moves the other way. One macro can open a filter while it closes a reverb.
say.straight: Each mapped knob has its own min and max. Flip them and that knob moves the other way.
say.eli5: You can tell the big knob how far to turn each little knob, and even to turn one backwards.

deeper.title: racks in live
deeper.say: Select devices on a track and press Cmd+G on a Mac or Ctrl+G on Windows to put them in a rack. Inside, chains run side by side and Live mixes them together.

deeper.title: mapping
deeper.say: Right-click a parameter inside a rack and map it to a macro. Since Live 11 a rack can have up to 16 macros. Set each mapping's Min and Max so the knob only moves as far as you want.

deeper.title: don't overload
deeper.say: Mapping too many things to one macro turns it to mush. Two or three is often plenty.

say.mentor:
A macro is one knob mapped to several. Your lead is playing. Turn the big knob and cutoff, res and drive all move together, each over its own range. That's a rack macro: one hand, a whole sound change.
Tap the chips to choose what the macro turns: add send for space, add lfo for movement, take drive out. Save a setting as a, turn to somewhere new and save b, then jump between them. Keep the setting you like.
say.straight: One knob moving several. Pick which knobs it turns, save two settings, jump between them. Keep what you like.
say.eli5: One big knob turns lots of little knobs at once.

steps.q: What is a macro?
options: one knob that moves several knobs at once
steps.why: One twist, several changes.

whyWrong.1: Samples are recordings.
whyWrong.2: Eq is one effect a macro might control.
whyWrong.3: The master fader sets the whole song's level.

steps.q: What does a rack do?
steps.why: Several devices, one container, with macros on the front.

whyWrong.1: Recording is the arm button.
whyWrong.3: Racks don't change stereo.

steps.q: How can one macro open a filter while closing a reverb?
options: flip one range so its max is below its min
steps.why: A flipped range moves that knob the other way.

whyWrong.1: It all happens in one rack.
whyWrong.2: Tempo has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: Flipped ranges make it easy.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, sections. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: putting it all together

song.why: hearing your bass's whole chain at once shows how the mix tools add up to one sound

lessons.learn: How the tools of this path join up, your bass's chain from sound to mix, and a setup that gets out of your way.
youCan: shape a part with tools from the whole mix path
say what an audio interface and a template are
save a template in Live

say.mentor: You've met levels, eq, effects, sends, glue and the limiter one at a time. In a real song they all work at once, on every part. Putting it all together means knowing which tool does which job, and setting things up so you can reach for it without thinking.
say.straight: In a real mix every tool works at once. Know which does what, and set up so you can reach it fast.
say.eli5: You've learned lots of tools. Now you use them all together on your song.

say.mentor:
A working setup is a few pieces joined up: a computer running a music program, an audio interface, which is the box that gets sound in and out of the computer, a midi controller to play, and speakers or headphones to listen.
The goal is to open a new song and be making music in under a minute. Producers get there with templates: a starting song with their usual tracks, sends and sounds already set up.
say.straight: Computer, audio interface (sound in and out), midi controller, speakers. A template is a ready-made starting song, so you start fast.
say.eli5: You need a computer, a box for sound, something to play and something to listen on. A template is a song that's already set up, so you can start right away.

deeper.title: templates in live
deeper.say: Set up your usual tracks, returns and devices, then choose Save Live Set As Template from the File menu. Every new set starts from it.

deeper.title: map your controller
deeper.say: Map your controller's play, stop and record buttons, and the knobs you reach for most, so your hands stay off the mouse.

deeper.title: back it up
deeper.say: Back up your projects automatically, and keep a list of your plugin licences. Moving things to a new drive can break them.

say.mentor:
Your bass, with one knob from each part of the path. Cutoff is the sound itself. Drive is an effect. Low is eq. Duck is the mix, dipping your bass under the kick.
Set them one at a time, then play with all four together. Notice how changing one changes what the others need. That's mixing.
say.straight: Cutoff (sound), drive (effect), low (eq), duck (mix). Set each, then adjust them together.
say.eli5: Four knobs for your bass. Turn each one, then turn them together until your bass sounds great with the kick.

steps.q: What does an audio interface do?
options: gets sound in and out of the computer
steps.why: It's the box between your computer and your speakers, mics and instruments.

whyWrong.1: You write the melodies.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is set in the music program.

steps.q: What is a template?
options: a starting song with your usual tracks and sends set up
steps.why: It saves you setting up from scratch every time.

whyWrong.1: A template is a starting point.
whyWrong.3: A template can hold patterns, but it's a whole setup.

steps.q: Why set the knobs one at a time, then adjust them together?
options: each tool changes what the others need
the knobs only work one at a time
steps.why: Every move shifts the balance, so you check them together.

whyWrong.1: They all work at once.
whyWrong.3: They all count.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, sections. Your loop becomes a song.

lessons.title: arrangement view

song.why: laying your sections out left to right gives your loop a beginning, a middle and an end

lessons.learn: The timeline, how a song is laid out from left to right, and your sections arranged on it.
youCan: read a song laid out on a timeline
arrange your parts across sections
switch between Live's two views

say.mentor:
There are two ways to look at a song. One is a set of loops you can launch in any order, great for jamming. The other is a timeline: the whole song laid out from left to right, first bar to last, like a line of text.
Live calls the timeline arrangement view, and it's where a loop becomes a finished song.
say.straight: Two ways to see a song: loops to launch, or a timeline from start to finish. The timeline is arrangement view.
say.eli5: A timeline shows your whole song in a line, from the start on the left to the end on the right.

say.mentor:
On a timeline, each part is a lane running across, and time moves from left to right. You can see at a glance where the drums drop out, how long the break lasts and where the drop lands.
Sections tend to come in 8 or 16 bar blocks, so changes land where dancers and djs expect them.
say.straight: Each part is a lane, time runs left to right. Sections usually come in 8 or 16 bar blocks.
say.eli5: Each sound gets its own row. You read it from left to right, like a book.

deeper.title: two views in live
deeper.say: Live has Session view, a grid of clips you launch, and Arrangement view, the timeline. Press Tab to switch between them.

deeper.title: recording a jam
deeper.say: Turn on Arrangement Record in the transport and play. Live records the clips you launch in Session view onto the timeline.

deeper.title: back to arrangement
deeper.say: Launch a Session clip while the arrangement plays and that track follows the clip instead. The Back to Arrangement button lights up. Click it and the timeline takes over again.

deeper.title: locators
deeper.say: Add a locator from the Create menu to mark where each section starts, then jump between them.

say.mentor:
Here's your song as a timeline: sections from left to right, each with its length in bars, and the total running time at the top. Each row is one of your parts.
Switch a few parts off in the intro and the break, then play it through and watch the playhead travel across your song.
say.straight: Sections left to right, parts as rows. Switch parts off in the intro and break, then play it through.
say.eli5: Tap squares to turn sounds off in some parts of your song. Press play and watch it move from left to right.

steps.q: On a timeline, which way does time run?
steps.why: First bar on the left, last bar on the right.

whyWrong.1: Parts are stacked top to bottom. Time runs across.
whyWrong.3: The playhead travels across it.

steps.q: What is arrangement view for?
options: laying out the whole song from start to finish
steps.why: It's the timeline, where the finished song lives.

whyWrong.1: That's Session view.
whyWrong.3: Eq lives on each track.

steps.q: In Live, which key switches between Session and Arrangement view?
steps.why: Tab flips between the two.

whyWrong.1: Space starts and stops playback.
whyWrong.2: A shows automation in Arrangement view.
whyWrong.3: Enter isn't the view switch.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, variation and fills.

lessons.title: scenes and follow actions

song.why: starting with drums alone and then bringing everything in is how a set builds, row by row

lessons.learn: Scenes, rows of clips launched together, follow actions, and your song built from drums alone up to everything.
youCan: say what a scene is
say what a follow action does
build a section of drums alone, then everything

say.mentor:
In Session view, Live lays your clips out as a grid: each part is a column, and each row is a scene. Launch a scene and every clip in that row starts together, right on the beat.
Build one row with drums alone and the next with everything, and you can play your song section by section, live.
say.straight: A scene is a row of clips that launch together. One row of drums, one row of everything, and you can play your song live.
say.eli5: A scene is a row of sounds that all start at once. Press one row, then the next, and your song builds up.

say.mentor:
A follow action tells a clip what to do when it finishes: play the next clip, play again, play any clip at random, or stop.
Chain them and a set keeps moving on its own, changing every few bars without you touching anything. Give two actions a chance each and it becomes unpredictable, a slightly different song every time.
say.straight: A follow action says what happens when a clip ends: next, again, random, stop. Chance makes it unpredictable.
say.eli5: A follow action tells a sound what to do when it's finished, like play the next one.

deeper.title: follow actions in live
deeper.say: The choices include Stop, Play Again, Previous, Next, First, Last, Any, Other and Jump. Each clip has two slots, A and B, each with its own chance.

deeper.title: tempo in a scene name
deeper.say: Put a tempo in a scene's name, like 128 BPM, and Live jumps to that tempo when the scene launches. A time signature like 6/8 works too.

say.mentor: Here's your song as sections, which play one after another like scenes. Make the first one drums alone: switch everything but your drums off there. Leave the next one with everything on. Play it and hear the change land on the beat.
say.straight: First section: drums only. Next: everything. Play it and hear the change.
say.eli5: In the first part, turn off everything except the drums. Leave the next part full. Press play.

steps.q: What is a scene?
options: a row of clips launched together
steps.why: Launch the row and every clip in it starts at once.

whyWrong.1: A scene holds clips for many parts.
whyWrong.3: The master is where everything ends up.

steps.q: What does a follow action do?
options: tells a clip what to do when it finishes
steps.why: Next, again, random or stop, chosen when the clip ends.

whyWrong.1: That's the fader.
whyWrong.3: Recording is the arm and record buttons.

steps.q: What happens when a scene named 128 BPM launches?
steps.why: Live reads the tempo from the scene's name.

whyWrong.1: The name sets tempo, not level.
whyWrong.3: Live reads tempos in scene names.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, variation and fills.

lessons.title: tracks

song.why: switching parts on and off is the quickest way to hear what each one adds

lessons.learn: What a track is, the kinds Live has, and your parts muted section by section.
youCan: say what mute, solo and arm do
name the kinds of track
mute parts in sections of your song

say.mentor:
Every part of your song lives on its own track: a lane with its own sound, its own fader and its own buttons. Kick, clap, hats, bass, lead, chords.
Three buttons you'll use all the time: mute silences a track, solo plays it alone, and arm gets it ready to record.
say.straight: Each part is a track. Mute silences it, solo plays it alone, arm gets it ready to record.
say.eli5: Every sound has its own row, called a track. Each track has buttons to make it quiet, play it alone, or get it ready to record.

say.mentor:
Not every track is the same. A midi track holds notes and needs an instrument to make a sound. An audio track holds recorded sound, like a sample or a vocal. A return holds a shared effect, a group holds other tracks, and the master is where everything ends up.
Pick the right kind for the job: audio goes on audio tracks, notes go on midi tracks.
say.straight: Midi tracks: notes plus an instrument. Audio tracks: recorded sound. Returns: shared effects. Groups: other tracks. Master: the sum.
say.eli5: Some tracks hold notes, some hold recordings. One special track, the master, holds everything.

deeper.title: new tracks in live
deeper.say: Cmd+T on a Mac or Ctrl+T on Windows makes a new audio track. Add Shift for a new midi track. A new midi track stays silent until you give it an instrument.

deeper.title: groups
deeper.say: Select tracks and press Cmd+G or Ctrl+G to put them in a group with one fader. Groups have their own automation.

deeper.title: colours
deeper.say: Colour tracks by job, drums one colour and synths another, so a big set stays easy to read.

say.mentor: Here's your song with every track as a row. Tap a cell to mute that track in that section. Mute your bass in the intro and your lead in the break. Play it through and hear how each part coming back lifts the next section.
say.straight: Tap a cell to mute a track in a section. Mute the bass in the intro, the lead in the break, then play it.
say.eli5: Tap the squares to make sounds quiet in some parts of your song. Press play and listen to them come back.

steps.q: What does arm do?
options: gets a track ready to record
steps.why: Arm a track, press record, and it records.

whyWrong.1: That's mute.
whyWrong.3: Arm never deletes anything.

steps.q: Where do notes go?
options: a midi track, with an instrument
steps.why: Midi tracks hold notes, and the instrument turns them into sound.

whyWrong.1: Audio tracks hold recorded sound.
whyWrong.3: Returns hold shared effects.

steps.q: What does a return track hold?
steps.why: Usually a reverb or delay that many tracks send to.

whyWrong.1: Drums go on their own tracks.
whyWrong.3: Tempo belongs to the whole set.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, variation and fills.

lessons.title: automation

song.why: a filter opening slowly over a few bars builds tension in your song

lessons.learn: What automation is, how it moves a knob over time, and your lead's cutoff swept by hand.
youCan: say what automation and breakpoints are
sweep a filter like automation would
show automation lanes in Live

say.mentor: A song that never changes gets dull fast. Automation is a knob moving on its own over time: a filter slowly opening over 8 bars, a fade in, a reverb swelling before a drop. You draw the move once and the song plays it back exactly the same, every time.
say.straight: Automation moves a knob over time, like a filter opening over 8 bars. Draw it once, it plays every time.
say.eli5: Automation is like a robot that turns a knob for you while the song plays, the same way every time.

say.mentor:
Automation is drawn as a line under a part, with breakpoints, the dots where the line changes direction. Line goes up, knob goes up. Flat line, the knob holds still.
A filter sweep is the classic: cutoff low and muffled at the start of a build, wide open at the drop.
say.straight: A line with breakpoints, the dots where it changes. Up is more, flat is still. The classic move is a filter sweep into a drop.
say.eli5: You draw a line. When the line goes up, the knob goes up. When it's flat, the knob stays still.

deeper.title: automation in live
deeper.say: In Arrangement view, press A to show automation lanes. Pick a parameter from a lane's menu and click to add breakpoints, or move the knob while recording and Live writes the line for you.

deeper.title: re-enable automation
deeper.say: Touch an automated knob by hand and it stops following its line until you click Re-Enable Automation. If a knob won't do what you set, this is usually why.

deeper.title: clip envelopes
deeper.say: In Session view, automation lives inside a clip as a clip envelope, so it travels with the clip.

deeper.title: curves
deeper.say: Since Live 11 you can bend automation lines into curves instead of straight ramps.

say.mentor:
Automation is a knob moving by itself over time, drawn as a line. The closest thing to a drawn line that repeats is an lfo, and your lead has one. Turn lfo up and set lfo rate very slow: the cutoff now rises and falls over a few bars on its own, like a long automation curve.
Set cutoff where the middle of the sweep should sit. lfo to on the volume gives a slow fade in and out instead. In Live you'd draw this in the automation lane; here the shape repeats every cycle. Keep the movement in your song.
say.straight: A slow lfo is a repeating automation curve. Turn it up, set the rate slow, choose what it moves. Keep it.
say.eli5: Automation is a knob that moves by itself. A slow wobble does that for you.

steps.q: What is automation?
options: a knob moving on its own over time
steps.why: Draw the move once and it plays back every time.

whyWrong.1: A kick's level is just a knob setting.
whyWrong.2: Reverb is an effect you might automate.
whyWrong.3: A fill is notes, not a knob moving.

steps.q: What's a breakpoint?
options: a dot where the automation line changes
steps.why: The line runs from dot to dot.

whyWrong.1: A gap would be silence.
whyWrong.3: Muting is a button.

steps.q: You moved an automated knob by hand and now it won't follow its line. Why?
options: touching it paused the automation until you re-enable it
steps.why: Click Re-Enable Automation and it follows the line again.

whyWrong.1: Nothing's broken.
whyWrong.2: Tempo has nothing to do with it.
whyWrong.3: It plays every time.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, variation and fills.

lessons.title: modulation lanes

song.why: your lead's level is the base a modulation lane wobbles around, so set it where it belongs

lessons.learn: How modulation differs from automation, and your lead's level set as the base a modulation lane moves around.
youCan: say how modulation and automation differ
say what happens when modulation goes past a knob's range
set the base level of your lead

say.mentor:
Automation sets a knob to an exact value: at one bar the level is here, eight bars later it's there. Modulation works differently. It adds or takes away a bit from wherever the knob already is.
So you can set your lead's level by hand, and a modulation lane wobbles it a little up and down around that spot.
say.straight: Automation sets a value. Modulation adds to or takes from the value you set.
say.eli5: Automation tells the knob exactly where to go. Modulation just wiggles it a little around where you left it.

say.mentor:
Because modulation is added on top, the knob stays yours. Turn the level up and the whole wobble moves up with it.
A modulation lane is drawn around a centre line. On the line, nothing changes. Above it adds, below it takes away. If the total would go past the top or bottom of the knob, it stops there.
say.straight: Modulation rides on top of your setting. Centre line is no change, above adds, below subtracts. It stops at the knob's limits.
say.eli5: The wiggle follows your knob. Turn the knob up and the wiggle goes up too.

deeper.title: modulation in live
deeper.say: In a clip's envelopes, a switch next to the chosen parameter flips the lane between automation and modulation.

deeper.title: which one when
deeper.say: Use automation for fixed moves that should happen the same way every time. Use modulation when you want movement but still want the knob free to tweak, like in a set you perform.

deeper.title: both at once
deeper.say: You can automate a knob's base value and modulate around it at the same time.

say.mentor:
Modulation lanes in Live 12 add movement on top of a value without replacing it. The lfo here does the same: level is the value you set, and the lfo moves around it.
Set lfo to the volume, lfo up a little, and the level pulses around where you left it. Change level and the pulse moves with it, which is the whole idea: the modulation is relative. Keep a gentle pulse or none.
