say.straight: The lfo adds movement around the level you set. Change level and the movement moves with it. That's a modulation lane.
say.eli5: Set the loudness, then let the wobble move around it.

steps.q: How is modulation different from automation?
options: modulation adds to the knob, automation sets it
steps.why: Modulation rides on your setting. Automation replaces it.

whyWrong.1: One sets, one adds.
whyWrong.3: Automation follows the line you draw.

steps.q: You turn the knob up while modulation is on. What happens?
options: the whole wobble moves up with it
steps.why: Modulation is added to wherever the knob is.

whyWrong.1: The lane stays.
whyWrong.3: The base moves, so everything moves.

steps.q: What happens if the knob plus modulation goes past the top?
options: it wraps round to the bottom
steps.why: It's held at the knob's limit.

whyWrong.1: It doesn't wrap.
whyWrong.3: It can't go past the top.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, variation and fills.

lessons.title: midi transformations

song.why: changing a bar of notes you already have is a fast way to make a fill

lessons.learn: What midi transformations are, the ones Live 12 has, and fills made from your own beat.
youCan: say what a midi transformation does
name a few of Live 12's transformations
place fills in your song

say.mentor:
Midi is notes, not sound: which note, when, how long and how hard. Because it's just notes, a program can change them for you. Spread a chord out like a strum, turn it into a run of notes, shuffle a rhythm. That's a midi transformation.
A fill is often exactly this: your normal beat, changed for one bar.
say.straight: Midi is notes. A transformation changes notes you already have. A fill is often your beat, changed for a bar.
say.eli5: Midi is a list of notes. The computer can shuffle and change that list for you, like magic.

say.mentor:
Live 12 has transformations built into its midi editing. Select some notes, pick one, and Live reshapes them. Strum spreads a chord's notes out in time, like a guitar. Arpeggiate turns a held chord into a run of single notes. Recombine shuffles the rhythm and the pitches separately. Ornament adds little grace notes.
You can try one and adjust it before you commit, so it's easy to try a few and pick.
say.straight: Strum spreads a chord in time. Arpeggiate turns it into single notes. Recombine shuffles rhythm and pitch. Ornament adds grace notes. Try before you commit.
say.eli5: Strum makes a chord sound like a guitar. Arpeggiate plays the chord one note at a time.

deeper.title: a starting point
deeper.say: Treat a transformation as a starting point. Apply Arpeggiate, then edit the notes it made by hand.

deeper.title: strum needs chords
deeper.say: Strum only makes sense on two or more notes played together. On a single line there's nothing to spread.

deeper.title: in your scale
deeper.say: When a transformation makes new pitches, it follows the scale you've set for the song.

say.mentor: Here's your song with a fill row. A fill here is your beat changed for its last beat: the kick drops out and a snare roll takes over. Tap fill on the sections that lead into a change, and hear how the changed bar sets up what's next.
say.straight: Tap fill on sections that lead into a change. The last beat becomes a snare roll.
say.eli5: Tap fill on the part before a big change. Listen to the drum roll.

steps.q: What does a midi transformation do?
steps.why: It reshapes your notes instead of you editing each one.

whyWrong.1: It works on midi notes, not recordings.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the song's speed.

steps.q: What does Strum do?
options: spreads a chord's notes out in time
steps.why: Like a guitarist's pick moving across the strings.

whyWrong.1: The notes stay notes.
whyWrong.3: The chord stays, just spread out.

steps.q: Why does Strum do nothing useful on a single melody line?
options: there's only one note at a time to spread
steps.why: Strum spreads notes that start together. One note has nothing to spread.

whyWrong.1: It's for chords, not drums.
whyWrong.3: It works on midi notes.

steps.next: Back to your song: next on the path, the breakdown and the drop.

lessons.title: groove pool

song.why: a groove pushes some of your hats a little late, and your beat starts to bounce

lessons.learn: What groove is, how Live's groove pool copies feel from one clip to another, and swing on your song.
youCan: say what groove is
say what the groove pool does
swing your hats by ear

say.mentor:
Every great loop has a feel. Some notes land a hair early or late against the grid, some hits are harder than others. That feel is called groove.
Listen: the same beat played straight, then swung. Same notes, but the second one moves.
say.straight: Groove is the feel: notes slightly off the grid, some harder than others. Straight, then swung.
say.eli5: Listen to the same beat twice. The second one bounces. That bounce is called groove.

say.mentor:
Live's groove pool lets you copy the feel out of one clip and put it on another. Drag a clip into it and Live makes a groove from where its notes land and how hard they hit. Drop that groove on your hats and they pick up the same feel.
Swing is the simplest groove there is: every off sixteenth pushed a little late.
say.straight: The groove pool copies the timing and hit strength of one clip onto another. Swing is the simplest groove: off sixteenths pushed late.
say.eli5: You can copy the bounce from one beat and stick it on another.

deeper.title: groove settings
deeper.say: A groove has a few controls. Timing sets how strongly it moves notes, Velocity how strongly it changes how hard they hit, and Random adds a small difference to each note. Base sets which note length it works on, and Quantize how much the notes snap to the grid first.

deeper.title: commit
deeper.say: Commit writes the groove into the notes for good. After that, the clip no longer follows the groove.

deeper.title: not on everything
deeper.say: The same groove at full strength on every part can make everything feel the same. Many producers use it lightly, on a few parts.

say.mentor:
Here's your song with a swing knob. Turn it up and listen to your hats: the off sixteenths start to land late and the beat begins to bounce. Your kick and clap stay where they are.
A little is a gentle shuffle, a lot is a heavy one. Stop where it makes you want to move.
say.straight: Swing pushes the off sixteenths late. Kick and clap stay put. Stop where it feels good.
say.eli5: Turn swing up and your hats start to bounce. Stop when it makes you want to dance.

steps.q: What is groove?
options: the feel of where notes land and how hard they hit
steps.why: Timing and hit strength, just off the grid.

whyWrong.1: Key is about which notes.
whyWrong.3: Bars are length.

steps.q: What does the groove pool do?
options: copies the feel of one clip onto another
steps.why: Drag in a clip, then apply its groove anywhere.

whyWrong.1: Samples live in the browser.
whyWrong.3: Recording is a different job.

steps.q: What does swing move?
options: the off sixteenths, a little late
steps.why: Kick and clap stay put. The notes in between move.

whyWrong.1: Kicks on the beat don't move.
whyWrong.3: It moves any part on those off sixteenths.

lessons.title: take lanes

song.why: recording a part a few times and keeping the best pass is how most great performances are made

lessons.learn: What a take is, how take lanes keep every pass, and your clap recorded as takes until one feels right.
youCan: say what a take is
say what take lanes keep
record a part as takes and keep the best

say.mentor:
Most great recorded performances aren't one perfect pass. They're the same part played again and again, with the best moments kept. Each pass is called a take.
Pros don't play it perfectly. They play it a few times and choose.
say.straight: A take is one recorded pass. Great performances are usually several takes, with the best one kept.
say.eli5: A take is one try at playing something. You can have lots of tries and keep the best one.

say.mentor: Take lanes are extra rows under a track. Each time you loop-record, the new pass lands on its own row and the old ones stay underneath. Nothing gets thrown away, so you can listen back and choose, today or tomorrow.
say.straight: Take lanes put each recorded pass on its own row under the track. Nothing is deleted.
say.eli5: Every try gets its own row, and none of them get thrown away.

deeper.title: take lanes in live
deeper.say: Right-click a track's header and choose Show Take Lanes. Loop a section and record: every pass round the loop lands on a new lane. They work for audio and midi, and arrived in Live 11.

deeper.title: name them
deeper.say: Name your lanes as you go, so future you knows which take was which.

say.mentor:
Take lanes keep every pass you record. Play your drums and keep the take, then do it again, up to three times. Each take sits in its own lane.
Then comp: the loop is split into four pieces, and for each piece you tap the lane whose playing was best. The light bar shows which piece is playing. Build a part from the best quarter of each take. In Live, this is take lanes and the comping tool, and it works exactly like this. Keep the comp.
say.straight: Record up to three takes of your drums. Then, for each quarter of the loop, pick the take that was best. Keep the comp.
say.eli5: Play it three times. Then build the best version from the best bits.

steps.q: What is a take?
options: one recorded pass of a part
steps.why: Play it once, that's a take. Play it again, that's another.

whyWrong.1: Eq is tone.
whyWrong.2: A take can be a pattern, but it's about one recorded pass.
whyWrong.3: The master adds everything up.

steps.q: What happens to old takes in take lanes?
options: they stay on their own rows underneath
steps.why: Every pass is kept, so you can choose later.

whyWrong.1: Nothing is thrown away.
whyWrong.3: Their level doesn't change.

lessons.title: comping

song.why: a bass line built from your best playing is better than any single pass

lessons.learn: What comping is, how the best pieces of each take become one, and a new take of your bass.
youCan: say what comping is
say why the joins get crossfades
record a bass take and choose whether to keep it

say.mentor: Say you play your bass line four times. The first take has a great start, the third has the best ending. Comping, short for compiling, means building one finished take from the best pieces of each. The result is better than any single pass you played.
say.straight: Comping builds one take from the best pieces of several.
say.eli5: You play something a few times, then glue the best bits together into one great version.

say.mentor:
With every take lined up underneath, you pick the bits you want, bar by bar or phrase by phrase. They're copied up into the main lane, called the comp, and the same stretch of every other take goes quiet.
The joins get crossfades: one take fades out as the next fades in, very quickly, so you don't hear a click where they meet.
say.straight: Pick bits from each take. They're copied up to the comp. Crossfades hide the joins.
say.eli5: You choose the best bits and they get joined up. The joins fade into each other so you can't hear a click.

deeper.title: comping in live
deeper.say: With take lanes showing, drag across the part of a take you want. It moves up to the main lane, and the same stretch on the other lanes is muted. Clear the comp and the takes are all still there.

deeper.title: by ear
deeper.say: Comp by listening, not by looking at the waveform.

deeper.title: clicks at a join
deeper.say: If you hear a click where two takes meet, make the fade there longer.

deeper.title: consolidate
deeper.say: When you're happy, consolidate the comp into one clip before you export.

say.mentor:
Take lanes keep every pass you record. Play your bass and keep the take, then do it again, up to three times. Each take sits in its own lane.
Then comp: the loop is split into four pieces, and for each piece you tap the lane whose playing was best. The light bar shows which piece is playing. Build a part from the best quarter of each take. In Live, this is take lanes and the comping tool, and it works exactly like this. Keep the comp.
say.straight: Record up to three takes of your bass. Then, for each quarter of the loop, pick the take that was best. Keep the comp.
say.eli5: Play it three times. Then build the best version from the best bits.

steps.q: What is comping?
options: building one take from the best pieces of several
steps.why: Short for compiling, the best bits of every take in one.

whyWrong.1: That's a compressor.
whyWrong.2: It's your own takes, not someone's song.
whyWrong.3: Swing is timing.

steps.q: Why do the joins in a comp get crossfades?
options: so you don't hear a click where takes meet
steps.why: A quick fade smooths the switch from one take to the next.

whyWrong.1: Level stays the same.
whyWrong.3: The notes don't change.

steps.q: Should you comp by eye or by ear?
steps.why: What matters is how it sounds.

whyWrong.1: A waveform can look fine and sound wrong.
whyWrong.3: Listening gives far better comps.

lessons.title: comping flow

song.why: a lead you've played a few times and chosen from sounds played, not programmed

lessons.learn: A comping routine that works, record everything first and choose later, and your lead recorded as takes.
youCan: record all your takes before judging them
narrow takes down to the best few
record a lead take and choose whether to keep it

say.mentor:
Comping well is mostly about routine. Get all your takes down first, while you're in the flow of playing. Then stop, take a break, and choose with fresh ears.
Picking while you're still recording makes you judge every note, and you start playing stiffly.
say.straight: Record every take first, choose later with fresh ears. Judging while you play makes you stiff.
say.eli5: First play lots of times without stopping. Choose the best one later.

say.mentor:
Record more takes than you need. Then narrow down: find the best two or three by ear, and comp only from those. Fewer choices, faster decisions.
Comp in sections. A quiet opening may want a gentler take than the big ending.
say.straight: Record plenty, narrow to the best two or three, then comp section by section.
say.eli5: Pick your favourite two or three tries, then choose the best bits from just those.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Loop recording makes a new take lane on every pass. With take lanes showing, a normal recording makes a new lane too. Each lane shows which bits of it are in the comp.

deeper.title: don't flatten early
deeper.say: Keep the take lanes until the song is finished. They're your safety net.

deeper.title: midi too
deeper.say: Comping works on midi takes as well, so you can pick the best chord voicings bar by bar.

say.mentor:
Take lanes keep every pass you record. Play your lead and keep the take, then do it again, up to three times. Each take sits in its own lane.
Then comp: the loop is split into four pieces, and for each piece you tap the lane whose playing was best. The light bar shows which piece is playing. Build a part from the best quarter of each take. In Live, this is take lanes and the comping tool, and it works exactly like this. Keep the comp.
say.straight: Record up to three takes of your lead. Then, for each quarter of the loop, pick the take that was best. Keep the comp.
say.eli5: Play it three times. Then build the best version from the best bits.

steps.q: Why record every take before choosing?
options: judging while you play makes you stiff
steps.why: Stay in the flow, then judge with fresh ears.

whyWrong.1: You can choose as often as you like.
whyWrong.3: Tempo doesn't change.

steps.q: How do you make comping decisions faster?
options: narrow to the best two or three takes first
steps.why: Fewer choices, faster decisions.

whyWrong.1: One take leaves nothing to choose from.
whyWrong.3: Louder doesn't help you choose.

steps.q: Why keep take lanes until the song is finished?
options: they're your safety net if you change your mind
steps.why: Once they're gone, so are the other takes.

whyWrong.1: The comp plays without them.
whyWrong.3: You can, which is why you wait.

lessons.title: macro variations

song.why: two versions of your drop give your song a second big moment

lessons.learn: Macro variations, saved snapshots of a rack's knobs, and two versions of your drop in your song.
youCan: say what a macro variation saves
say what happens to settings a variation doesn't cover
build two different drops

say.mentor: Once a sound has macros, you'll find settings you love: a dark version for the break, a bright one for the drop. A macro variation is a saved snapshot of every macro knob on a rack. Store one, change the knobs, store another, and you can jump between whole sounds in one click.
say.straight: A macro variation saves every macro on a rack. Store a few and jump between them in one click.
say.eli5: A variation is like taking a photo of where all your big knobs are, so you can go back to it in one tap.

say.mentor:
A variation only remembers the macros. Anything you haven't mapped to a macro stays where it is when you switch.
Many producers use them for sections: one variation per part of the song, so going from the break to the drop changes a whole sound at once.
say.straight: Variations only store macros. Unmapped settings don't change. Use one per section.
say.eli5: It only remembers the big knobs. Everything else stays the same.

deeper.title: variations in live
deeper.say: Macro Variations live in the rack, next to the macros. Set the macros, store a new variation, change them, store another. Click a variation to recall it. You can map switching to a controller, so one pad recalls one section.

say.mentor:
Macro variations are snapshots of all your macros. Set the big knob low, dark and dry, and save it as a. Turn it high, bright with movement, and save it as b.
Now tap a, tap b, in time with the song. That's what Live's variations do: store a whole rack state and recall it with one click, which is how one lead becomes a verse sound and a drop sound. Keep whichever state you want your lead to sit in.
say.straight: Save the macro low as a and high as b, then jump between them. That's a variation. Keep the state you want.
say.eli5: Save two settings. Flip between them. Two sounds from one lead.

steps.q: What is a macro variation?
options: a saved snapshot of a rack's macro knobs
steps.why: Store it, then recall every macro in one click.

whyWrong.1: It lives inside one rack.
whyWrong.3: Eq is an effect.

steps.q: You switch variations. What happens to settings not mapped to a macro?
steps.why: A variation only remembers the macros.

whyWrong.1: Nothing resets.
whyWrong.3: Nothing is deleted.

lessons.title: instrument rack

song.why: two voices stacked on your lead make it thicker and wider than one

lessons.learn: What an instrument rack is, layers and splits, and your lead thickened with a second voice.
youCan: say what layering and splitting are
say what key and velocity zones do
stack two voices on your lead

say.mentor: An instrument rack holds several instruments on one track. Play a note and every instrument inside plays it together. That's layering: a soft pad under a sharp lead, two synths stacked into one bigger sound.
say.straight: An instrument rack holds several instruments on one track. Layering plays them all at once.
say.eli5: An instrument rack is like two or three instruments playing the same note at the same time.

say.mentor:
Each instrument in a rack sits on its own chain, a row with its own instrument and effects. Chains can all play at once, which is a layer. Or each can answer only part of the keyboard, which is a split: low keys play a bass, high keys play chords.
Chains can also answer only soft or only hard hits, so a gentle touch plays one sound and a hard one plays another.
say.straight: Each instrument is a chain. All at once is a layer. Different keys for each is a split. Chains can also answer soft or hard hits.
say.eli5: You can play all the instruments together, or give each one its own part of the keyboard.

deeper.title: zones in live
deeper.say: Every chain in an Instrument Rack has a key zone, the notes it answers, and a velocity zone, the hit strengths it answers. A chain selector lets a macro choose which chains play, so one knob can move from one sound to another.

deeper.title: watch the overlap
deeper.say: Two chains playing the same notes both use processing power, and can clash. Overlap zones on purpose, not by accident.

deeper.title: glue the layers
deeper.say: A compressor after the rack helps layered chains sound like one instrument.

say.mentor:
An instrument rack layers instruments so one note plays several. Your lead is a layer of two already: an oscillator you set with shape and an fm voice. Turn fm up to half and you hear both at once, the warm wave under the glassy fm.
detune widens the oscillator layer, lfo gives the whole stack movement. That's a rack: two instruments, one note, one set of macros. Keep the blend.
say.straight: Two voices on one note: the oscillator and fm. Blend them with fm, widen with detune. That's a rack.
say.eli5: Two sounds play every time you press one key.

steps.q: What does an instrument rack let you do?
options: play several instruments from one track
steps.why: Several chains, one track.

whyWrong.1: Recording is a track's job.
whyWrong.3: Exporting happens from the File menu.

steps.q: What is a split?
options: chains answering different parts of the keyboard
steps.why: Low keys play one sound, high keys another.

whyWrong.1: It's one instrument track.
whyWrong.3: Fills are notes in a pattern.

steps.q: What does a velocity zone decide?
options: which hit strengths a chain answers
steps.why: Soft hits can play one chain, hard hits another.

whyWrong.1: Velocity is how hard, not how fast the song is.
whyWrong.3: Reverb is a separate effect.

lessons.title: exporting from live

song.why: an export is the moment your song becomes a file anyone can play

lessons.learn: What exporting is, audio files, stems and midi, and your song named and exported.
youCan: say the difference between an audio and a midi export
choose a format for a master and for sharing
export your song

say.mentor: Exporting turns your song into a file that lives outside the program. There are two main kinds. An audio export is the finished sound, a file anyone can play. A midi export is the notes, which another program can play on its own instruments.
say.straight: Exporting makes a file of your song. Audio is the finished sound. Midi is the notes.
say.eli5: Exporting turns your song into a file you can send to anyone.

say.mentor:
Wav and aiff are full quality, so keep one as your master copy. Mp3 is smaller and fine for sharing, but it throws a little detail away, so it shouldn't be your master.
Stems are each part, or group of parts, exported as its own audio file. They're for collaborators, remixers and mastering engineers.
say.straight: Wav or aiff for your master, mp3 for sharing. Stems are each part as its own audio file.
say.eli5: Keep a best-quality copy of your song, and a smaller one to share. You can also save each sound on its own.

deeper.title: export in live
deeper.say: Choose Export Audio/Video from the File menu, or press Cmd+Shift+R on a Mac or Ctrl+Shift+R on Windows. Pick what to render, the master or individual tracks, the format (WAV, AIFF, FLAC or MP3), the sample rate and the bit depth.

deeper.title: set the range
deeper.say: Live renders the length you've selected, so set it to cover the whole song. Forget, and you'll get only part of it.

deeper.title: stems in live
deeper.say: Render All Individual Tracks to export every track as its own file.

deeper.title: hardware
deeper.say: If hardware synths are part of your song, turn on real-time rendering so Live plays them while it exports.

deeper.title: headroom
deeper.say: For a streaming master, many engineers leave about 1 dB of headroom rather than pushing the peak right up to the top.

say.mentor: Here's your finished song. Give it a name, play it through once more, and download the midi: the notes of every part, ready to drop into Live, where each part lands on its own track and plays on Live's instruments.
say.straight: Name it, play it through, download the midi, open it in Live.
say.eli5: Type a name for your song, then tap download.

steps.q: Which file should you keep as your master copy?
steps.why: Full quality. Make smaller copies from it.

whyWrong.1: Mp3 throws a little detail away.
whyWrong.3: Midi is notes, not the finished sound.

steps.q: What are stems?
options: each part exported as its own audio file
steps.why: Drums, bass, lead and so on, each in its own file.

whyWrong.1: That's midi.
whyWrong.3: Stems are sound files.

steps.q: What does a midi export hold?
steps.why: Which notes, when, how long and how hard.

whyWrong.1: That's an audio export.
whyWrong.3: It's music data only.

lessons.title: live sets and projects

song.why: a song saved and named properly is a song you can come back to

lessons.learn: What a Live Set and a project are, how to save so nothing goes missing, and your song given a proper name.
youCan: say what a Live Set and a project are
save versions instead of saving over
collect a set's files into its project in Live

say.mentor: In Live, your song is saved as a Live Set, a single file ending in .als. But a song is more than that file. It also uses samples and presets stored in other places. The project is the folder around the set that keeps all of it together.
say.straight: A Live Set is your song's file (.als). The project is the folder that holds it and everything it uses.
say.eli5: Your song is saved as a file, and the file lives in a folder with all the sounds it needs.

say.mentor:
The habit that saves you: the first time you save a song, put it in its own new folder named after the song. Before you close or move it, collect everything the song uses into that folder.
Save new versions as you go, version 1, 2, 3, instead of saving over the same file. If a change goes wrong, the last good one is still there.
say.straight: One song, one new folder. Collect everything into it. Save numbered versions instead of saving over.
say.eli5: Give every song its own folder. Save a new copy each time, so you can always go back.

deeper.title: collect all and save
deeper.say: Collect All and Save, in the File menu, copies every sample the set uses into its project folder, so you can move it or send it to someone and it still opens.

deeper.title: manage project
deeper.say: In the File menu, Manage Files then Manage Project lists missing samples and unused ones, so you can tidy up before you archive.

deeper.title: templates
deeper.say: Save Live Set As Template stores your usual starting setup: tracks, sends and devices.

deeper.title: crash recovery
deeper.say: Crash recovery isn't a save. It's a one-time rescue after a crash, so save often.

say.mentor: Here's your song. Saving starts with a name. Give it a real one, not my song, and download the midi as your first saved copy. In Live, this is the moment you'd make the song its own folder.
say.straight: Give your song a real name and download the midi as your first saved copy.
say.eli5: Give your song a name you like, then tap download to save a copy.

steps.q: What is a project in Live?
options: the folder that holds a set and everything it uses
steps.why: The set plus its samples and presets, all in one place.

whyWrong.1: A project holds samples, but it's the whole folder.
whyWrong.3: The fader sets level.

steps.q: Why save new versions instead of saving over one file?
options: if a change goes wrong, the last good one is still there
Live can only open new files
steps.why: Every version is a way back.

whyWrong.1: Live opens any saved set.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is saved with the song.

steps.q: What does Collect All and Save do?
options: copies every sample the set uses into its project folder
steps.why: Then the project works anywhere you move it.

whyWrong.1: Nothing is deleted.
whyWrong.3: That's Save Live Set As Template.

lessons.title: files and projects

song.why: knowing which file holds what means your song never breaks when you move it

lessons.learn: The files a song is made of, sets, projects, samples and packs, and your song as a file you can take anywhere.
youCan: say what a set, a project and a pack are
say why a part can go silent after a move
download your song as a midi file

say.mentor:
A song on a computer is a bundle of files. The set holds your arrangement and settings. Samples are separate audio files that the set points to. Move a sample, or the set, and the set may not find it. Then that part goes silent.
Knowing what's where is how you stop that happening.
say.straight: A song is several files. The set points to samples stored separately. Lose a sample and that part goes silent.
say.eli5: Your song is made of a few files. If one goes missing, part of your song goes quiet.

say.mentor:
A Live Set is one file, your song. A project is the folder around it that holds the set plus its samples and presets. A pack is a bundle made for sharing sounds, the way Ableton ships its own sound libraries.
One song, one project folder. Put every song in one big folder and the links between files get tangled when you move things.
say.straight: Set: your song. Project: the folder with the set and its sounds. Pack: a bundle for sharing. One song per project folder.
say.eli5: The song file goes in a folder with its sounds. Give every song its own folder.

deeper.title: projects in live
deeper.say: Live treats any folder with an Ableton Project Info folder inside as a project, and looks for samples relative to it first.

deeper.title: collect before you send
deeper.say: Use Collect All and Save before you send a project to someone, so every sample travels with it.

deeper.title: packs
deeper.say: A Live Pack is a single .alp file. Ableton uses packs to share sounds, and you can make your own.

say.mentor: Here's your song. The midi file you download is another kind of file: just the notes, no sound, which is why it's tiny. Name it, download it, and find it with your other files. It travels anywhere, and almost any music program can open it.
say.straight: Name your song and download the midi. It's just notes, so it's tiny and opens almost anywhere.
say.eli5: Name your song and tap download. You get a tiny file with all your notes in it.

steps.q: What happens if a set can't find a sample it uses?
steps.why: The set only points to the sample. No sample, no sound.

whyWrong.1: Live can't invent the missing sound.
whyWrong.3: The part that uses it can't play.

steps.q: What does a project folder hold?
options: the set plus its samples and presets
steps.why: Everything one song needs, in one place.

whyWrong.1: It holds what the set uses too.
whyWrong.3: Midi is just one kind of file it might hold.

steps.q: Why is a midi file so small?
options: it holds only notes, no sound
it's a shortcut to your song
steps.why: Notes are tiny compared with recorded sound.

whyWrong.1: There's no audio in it.
whyWrong.3: It's a real file you can open anywhere.

lessons.title: stem separation

song.why: hearing your parts one at a time is what stems are, and it shows what each part adds

lessons.learn: What stems are, how Live 12 can pull them out of a finished track, and your own song heard part by part.
youCan: say what a stem is
say what bleed is
hear your song as stems

say.mentor: A finished track is one blended sound, everything mixed together. Stems are the parts pulled apart again: the drums on their own, the bass on its own, and so on. Djs and producers use them to remix, to sample, and to learn how a track was built.
say.straight: Stems are a track's parts on their own: drums, bass and so on. Used for remixing, sampling and learning.
say.eli5: A song is lots of sounds mixed together. Stems are those sounds pulled apart again.

say.mentor:
Live 12 can separate a mixed audio clip into four stems, using a model that runs on your own computer, no internet needed.
It's never perfect. Expect some bleed: bits of one part leaking into another's stem, like a little kick left in the bass. Treat stems as a starting point.
Your own song is easier. Its parts were never mixed into one, so every part is already its own stem.
say.straight: Live 12 splits a mixed clip into four stems, on your computer. Expect bleed, parts leaking into each other. Your song's parts are already stems.
say.eli5: Live can pull a song apart into four pieces. The pieces aren't perfect, a bit of one sound leaks into another.

deeper.title: in live
deeper.say: Right-click an audio clip and choose to separate it into stems. Live makes a new audio clip for each stem, lined up in time with the original.

deeper.title: what separates well
deeper.say: Sparse electronic tracks separate cleanly. Dense, busy mixes are harder, and so are masters that have been limited very hard.

deeper.title: ideas
deeper.say: Pull the drums out of a track, slice them onto pads and play your own pattern. Or pull a bass line out of an old record to study it.

say.mentor: Here's your song as sections. Turn one section into a drums stem: switch everything off except your drums. Make the next one a bass stem, then let the last bring everything back. Play it through and hear each part alone, then all together.
say.straight: One section drums only, one bass only, then everything. Play it and hear the stems.
say.eli5: In one part, keep only the drums. In the next, only the bass. Then turn everything back on.

options: one part of a track on its own
steps.why: Drums alone, bass alone, and so on.

whyWrong.1: That's what stems are pulled from.
whyWrong.3: Tempo is the song's speed.

options: bits of one part leaking into another's stem
steps.why: Separation isn't perfect, so some sound ends up in the wrong stem.

whyWrong.1: Clipping is going over the top.
whyWrong.3: A fade is a change in level.

options: they were never mixed into one sound
steps.why: Each part was made on its own, so it's still on its own.

lessons.title: troubleshooting

song.why: switching parts off one at a time is how you find the one causing a problem

lessons.learn: How to track down a problem, the usual suspects in Live, and your song checked part by part.
youCan: find a problem by switching things off one at a time
say what usually causes crackles
know where Live's audio settings are

say.mentor: Sooner or later something goes wrong: no sound, crackles, a controller that won't respond. The fix is usually simple once you know where to look. The trick is to find which piece is at fault before you start changing things.
say.straight: No sound, crackles, a dead controller. Find which piece is at fault before changing anything.
say.eli5: When something goes wrong, first find out which bit is broken. Then fix just that bit.

say.mentor:
No sound: check the audio device, the master fader and where the output is going.
Crackles and pops: the computer can't keep up. The buffer is the chunk of sound the computer works on at a time. Raise the buffer size to give it more time, or lighten the load.
A controller doing nothing: check it's switched on in Live's midi settings.
say.straight: No sound: device, master fader, output. Crackles: raise the buffer size, the chunk the computer works on at once. Dead controller: check the midi settings.
say.eli5: If there's no sound, check the volume and the speakers. If it crackles, the computer is too busy, so give it more time.

deeper.title: where to look in live
deeper.say: Preferences, then Audio, holds the audio device, buffer size and sample rate. Live's CPU meter shows how hard the computer is working.

deeper.title: freeze
deeper.say: Right-click a heavy track and choose Freeze. Live renders it to audio so it stops working it out as it plays, which frees up the computer. Flatten makes that permanent.

deeper.title: midi controllers
deeper.say: In the Link, Tempo and MIDI preferences, switch on Track for your controller's input port.

say.mentor:
Here's your song as sections. Nothing's wrong with it, so practise the method. Pick a section and switch parts off one at a time, listening each time.
If something in your song ever sounds off, this is how you'd find it: whatever you switch off that takes the problem with it is the culprit.
say.straight: Switch parts off one at a time in a section and listen. That's how you find what's causing a problem.
say.eli5: Turn off one sound at a time and listen. If the problem goes away, you found it.

steps.q: What's the first step in fixing a problem?
options: find which piece is at fault
steps.why: Then you only fix what's broken.

whyWrong.1: Changing everything makes it harder to find.
whyWrong.3: Louder doesn't fix anything.

steps.q: Crackles and pops usually mean what?
options: the kick is out of tune
steps.why: Give it more time with a bigger buffer, or lighten the load.

whyWrong.1: Quiet songs don't crackle.
whyWrong.3: A long reverb sounds smooth.

steps.q: What does freezing a track do?
options: renders it to audio so the computer works less
steps.why: The computer plays the render instead of working it out live.

whyWrong.1: The track stays.
whyWrong.3: Level doesn't change.
